    #134008. “Borat 2” makes an America slathered in misogyny and disinformation reckon with itself

    📅 23 Oct 2020 • ⏱️ 10m • 📚 Deep Dive (1958 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Salon ↗ Open Full Page

    “Borat 2” makes an America slathered in misogyny and disinformation reckon with itself

    📅 23 Oct 2020 | ⏱️ 10 min read (1958 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Salon

    ⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • On Wednesday multiple news outlets revealed the purported headliner of “Borat Subsequent Moviefilm” to be none other than Rudy Giuliani, President Donald Trump’s trusted lawyer and cable news’s favorite nutcase.
    • Compared with the mock attempted kidnapping Pamela Anderson, Borat’s ultimate get in 2006’s “Borat: Cultural Learnings of America for Make Benefit Glorious Nation of Kazakhstan,” the pranking of America’s mayor does not make for a grand climax or even an affectionate one.
    • It has been revealed that all it took for the producers of “Borat Subsequent Moviefilm” to succeed in their mission was a simple honeytrap, presented in the form of Baron Cohen’s exceptional co-star Maria Bakalova dressed as a right-wing fake news Barbie.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    On Wednesday multiple news outlets revealed the purported headliner of “Borat Subsequent Moviefilm” to be none other than Rudy Giuliani, President Donald Trump’s trusted lawyer and cable news’s favorite nutcase.

    Compared with the mock attempted kidnapping Pamela Anderson, Borat’s ultimate get in 2006’s “Borat: Cultural Learnings of America for Make Benefit Glorious Nation of Kazakhstan,” the pranking of America’s mayor does not make for a grand climax or even an affectionate one. Instead, it more or less confirms what we already know about Rudy Giuliani: his corruptibility makes him shockingly easy to dupe.

    It has been revealed that all it took for the producers of “Borat Subsequent Moviefilm” to succeed in their mission was a simple honeytrap, presented in the form of Baron Cohen’s exceptional co-star Maria Bakalova dressed as a right-wing fake news Barbie. By the time we get to that scene the Bulgarian actor has solidly established that she is the reason this feminist-themed sequel works as well as it does.

    Recent findings suggest that performance-wise, Bakalova fully commits and never breaks, keeping pace with Baron Cohen in every shared sequence and commanding every scene she pilots solo. If Baron Cohen were to ever greenlight an inheritor to his Borat franchise, she would more than do it justice.

    And this illustrates the subtextual call to action throughout “Subsequent Movefilm” for women of good conscience to reclaim their power, not only at the polls but in the realm of social equity. Baron Cohen and his writers cloak this in slapstick from the moment we’re introduced to Bakalova’s Tutar, the 15-year-old daughter Borat never realized he had.

    In a recent development, tutar is filthy and coarse, raised in a pen and guided by a book given to her by the Kazakh government that insists that women cannot drive, own businesses or even touch their privates without causing great disaster on par with the sinking of the Titanic. Her highest aspiration is to live in a golden cage like Queen Melania, “the happiest wife in the world,” emboldening her to join Borat’s latest trip as a stowaway.

    Similarly life, and Borat’s government, have not been kind to him since “Cultural Learnings” conquered America with great success – high five! – 14 years ago.

    According to recent reports, america may have loved Borat but his countrymen, neighbors and family in his home village of Kuzcek felt great shame at how his documentary portrayed them (a nod, perhaps, at the Romanian villagers angered at being misrepresented in the 2006 film, who unsuccessfully sued its producers). In reaction he was sentenced to a life of hard labor in a gulag.

    When Kazakhstan’s current Premier Nazarbayev (Dani Popescu) realizes the regime has a use for Borat, he’s hauled out of prison, shaved into a familiar form – ill-fitting grey suit, walrus mustache, puffy hairstyle and all – and given a upcoming mission to smooth glorious leader’s entry into the world’s strongman club. How? By presenting to”Vice Premier Mikhail Pence” valuable offering: Johnny the Monkey, “Kazakhstan’s Minister of Culture and No.1 porno star.”.

    According to recent reports, this is why the Giuliani spoiler leaking before the film’s release fails to ruin “Borat Subsequent Moviefilm” because, like old Johnny would do in a room full of bananas,  plunking Giuliani into a situation like the one announced in the film’s full title: “Borat Subsequent Moviefilm: Delivery of Prodigious Bribe to American Regime for Make Benefit Once Glorious Nation of Kazakhstan” merely yields the expected results. Giuliani was hoodwinked not by a monkey but old-fashioned monkey business. Wa-wa-wee-wa!

    In the main, the humor driving “Borat Subsequent Moviefilm” is a continuation of what Baron Cohen does in his 2018 Showtime series “Who Is America?” – which is to say that he functions more as a prodding force these days than a hard crowbar. Long ago the Borat character functioned as a truth serum, the kind of amiable ignoramus people were inclined to countenance or forgive either out of politeness or a sense of superiority. Bigots would meet his bigotry with their own, perhaps, in a gesture of finding common ground, while others put up with him out of kindness.

    Now, as father and daughter embark travel through the good old U.S. of A, 2020 edition, they encounter a place where the rampant racism, anti-Semitism and Islamophobia Borat unearthed in 2006 is now on proud display across the land and slathered in misogyny.

    Sources indicate that the sexism, though, is the road by which Borat and Tutar find their way into the psyche of the ugly American – enabling them to infiltrate a debutante ball where Borat gets a father to admit he’d pay $500 for Tutar within earshot of his own child, and another man, hopelessly drunk, slurs out unbidden that men love pretty girls in South. “They’re fun!”.

    Recent findings suggest that following a span of time in which Borat keeps Tutar in a cage while he sleeps in the relative luxury of a horse trailer he drags behind a jalopy, “Subsequent Moviefilm” makes Tutar’s empowerment the centerpiece of the movie’s second half. Baron Cohen’s signature obviousness and a style reminiscent of director Jason Woliner’s past TV work (which includes series such as “Nathan for You”) shapes how this transpires, and the audience either accepts this for what it is or may cringe at its clunkiness.

    Either way, the fact that “Borat Subsequent Moviefilm” and Baron Cohen need Bakalova is indisputable.

    Recent findings suggest that there’s the practical matter that the character of Borat is famous, for one. Back in 2007 Baron Cohen announced that he was retiring two of his alter egos, Borat and Ali G, acknowledging to The Daily Telegraph that “the problem with success, although it’s fantastic, is that every new person who sees the Borat movie is one less person I ‘get’ with Borat again, so it’s a kind of self-defeating form, really.”.

    What he could not have predicted back then was how thoroughly the fabric of reality would be torn by the disinformation flood plaguing us today. However, he’s right about the problem of Borat’s fame. “Subsequent Moviefilm” confronts this early in the film when Borat sets down in America once again, only to be instantly recognized and pursued by crowds of thrilled Texans. This necessitates a trip to a local costume shop to purchase prosthetics and disguises.

    Nonetheless, Borat’s relevance in 2020 is debatable. Since the anti-Semitism and sexism at his heart are defining traits in a nation seized by white nationalism, that either makes him redundant or highly relevant — except for when he revealshis subjects’ prejudices.

    It has been revealed that but then, the laugh-until-you-cry parts of the original “Borat” don’t involve, say, the Islamophobic, homophobic rodeo organizer mouthing off or those Southern frat boys wishing aloud that slavery was still legal. The best antics involve Borat’s stupidity crashing against the patience and politeness of typical Americans, or ludicrous moments like the nude wrestling match between him and his producer Azamat (Ken Davilian) that spills out of their hotel room and well into public spaces.

    Fewer of those sight gags exist in “Subsequent Moviefilm.” Save for an extended segment in which he quarantines with a pair of right-wing QAnon adherents, they have been replaced instead by situational humor, such as when Tutar swallows a plastic baby cake decoration and Borat rushes her to what he believes to be a doctor’s office. Naturally they land in crisis pregnancy center where father and daughter are counseled, not by a doctor but by Pastor Jonathan Bright. This evolves precisely as one expects it would.

    Industry observers note that then there are the bits that have already made the news: Baron Cohen’s infiltrating the Conservative Political Action Conference in February dressed as Trump? They work their way to that, and a scene from a right-wing militia gathering in Washington state where Borat performed as Country Steve and got the audience to sing along to a racist ditty, starting with lyrics about injecting Obama “with the Wuhan flu.”.

    Recent findings suggest that gotcha moments like this and the Giuliani business don’t tell us anything we don’t already know. Instead, it’s what the context implies about America’s psychological state. The cringe comedy in the crisis center isn’t merely in the pastor’s misunderstanding about the nature of the baby inside Tutar’s stomach. It is his calm insistence in her keeping it there even after Tutar’s father tells him that he put it there. (He bought the cupcake, OK?).

    But this is part of an escalating series of moments that show us who America is: a nation of very fine people who live and let prejudice flourish so long as it doesn’t disturb the status quo.

    There’s the Texas baker who uses icing to pipe the words “Jews Will Not Replace Us” on a chocolate cake without batting an eyelash. There’s the shop owner who guffaws along with Borat when he asks that Tutar be directed to the “no means yes” dress section. There’s the spray tanning salon technician who, in response to Borat asking, “What color is best for racist family?” says without pause or reaction, “I wouldn’t go any darker than a six or a seven.”.

    All of these are women, by the way.

    In a recent development, this leads up to savior in this narrative: Jeanise Jones, a Black woman Borat hires to look after Tutar and who ends up talking some sense in to her, starting with waking her up to the fact that her father has been lying to her. (And how.) Jones is the level-headed figure in a vast land of fools; she’s also playing to the trope of the Black woman savior utilized in the first “Borat” and touted in this election cycle. Placed in the context of everyone else Borat and Tutar encounter, though, she’s a cool clarifying drink in a desert of dumb and therefore welcome.

    According to recent reports, evaluating the comedy value of “Subsequent Moviefilm” relative to the first “Borat” sets it up to lose, sad to say. It is enormously entertaining and, for the reasons listed above, a healthy treatment to whatever anxieties may be plaguing us a little more than a week leading up to the election. Whatever faults it has aren’t deadly, although it’s plain to see that the pandemic may have shifted the film’s ending in ways that don’t feel fully baked.

    Recent findings suggest that the most prominent difference between the “Borat” of 2006 and the 2020 “Subsequent Moviefilm” is in who America is now. Our inability to agree on basic facts has only worsened since Trump’s election in 2016, to say nothing of how decline and fall of basic critical thought has left us vulnerable to benevolent pranksters like Baron Cohen and outside forces who would mean us harm.

    Sources indicate that at the same time, there’s simply no getting around the fact that Kazakhstan receives little in the way of an image acquittal in this follow-up, an unavoidable and miserable result of alloying a problematic character to a place. If there’s a salvageable component to this, it is in how differently the sequel leaves us. When we first met Borat we comforted ourselves with the first-world notion that somehow we are better than people of so-called “lesser” nations.

    It has been revealed that now it doesn’t allow the audience to be so sure of itself, implying in the final scene that we aren’t merely ugly Americans. We’re a once glorious nation being led by goons who are sliding us backward into diminishment, and dangerously so. That is nothing to laugh about.

    “Borat Subsequent Moviefilm: Delivery of Prodigious Bribe to American Regime for Make Benefit Once Glorious Nation of Kazakhstan” is right now streaming on Amazon.

    #134006. “Chaos” in the air: Five ways voting could be disrupted on Election Day

    📅 03 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 12m • 📚 Deep Dive (2356 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Salon ↗ Open Full Page

    “Chaos” in the air: Five ways voting could be disrupted on Election Day

    📅 03 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2356 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Salon

    ⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • As Americans head to the polls on Tuesday, voting experts are watching to see how the Trump administration’s unprecedented efforts to assert more federal control over elections will play out.
    • Since President Donald Trump retook the White House, his administration has tried to force states to turn over their unredacted voter rolls and to restrict mail-in voting.
    • The president has justified these steps by claiming, without evidence, that American elections are beset by fraud and that illegal voting is tipping the scales in favor of Democrats.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    This article originally appeared on ProPublica.

    As Americans head to the polls on Tuesday, voting experts are watching to see how the Trump administration’s unprecedented efforts to assert more federal control over elections will play out.

    Since President Donald Trump retook the White House, his administration has tried to force states to turn over their unredacted voter rolls and to restrict mail-in voting. The Department of Homeland Security has used its resources to identify and prosecute noncitizen voters, an effort that has unfolded alongside the agency’s massive crackdown on immigrants.

    The president has justified these steps by claiming, without evidence, that American elections are beset by fraud and that illegal voting is tipping the scales in favor of Democrats.

    Industry observers note that courts have thwarted most of the administration’s plans to date, but Trump and his top deputies have kept up the pressure. Most recently, they’ve threatened to prosecute election officials who don’t reject ballots from people that the federal government has identified as likely noncitizens.

    The administration hasn’t explicitly ruled out sending federal agents to the polls or seizing ballots or voting machines.

    Election experts say the cumulative effect has been to ramp up anxiety about the midterms and to erode voters’ trust in the system.

    “The administration has been creating a lot of noise, a lot of confusion, a lot of doubt,” mentioned Ben Hovland, whom Trump fired as a commissioner for the bipartisan Election Assistance Commission earlier this year. He said he worries that this will make voters “sit it out” and “throw their hands up.”.

    In an emailed response to questions, a DHS spokesperson said Immigration and Customs Enforcement “is not planning operations targeting polling locations,” adding that the agency would only arrest people at the polls to address a safety threat as part of “intelligence-driven targeted enforcement.”.

    It has been revealed that the DHS and the Justice Department “are laser focused on identifying, prosecuting and removing aliens who vote and dilute the votes of U.S. citizens,” the spokesperson added. “Our message to aliens who vote in American elections is clear: we will find you, arrest you, and you will face the consequences — including criminal charges and deportation.”.

    Before and on Election Day, it’s typical for the major political parties to mount poll-watching operations, but both Democrats and Republicans say they’ve expanded these activities in this pressurized midterm.

    According to recent reports, republicans will focus on complications such as voter eligibility and voter-roll accuracy, according to Ally Triolo, the Republican National Committee’s election integrity communications director. Democrats will concentrate on voter intimidation and other hurdles to voting, Angelo Fernández Hernández, a Democratic National Committee spokesperson, said.

    Here are five issues that voting rights experts say they’re watching as this year’s election unfolds:.

    An incident in Leon County, in the Florida Panhandle, illustrates the widespread anxiety about law enforcement at the polls.

    Mark Earley, the county’s supervisor of elections, told ProPublica he was “furious” when two marked U.S. Customs and Border Protection vehicles parked outside the county’s busiest early voting location last month, after he’d been repeatedly reassured by the administration that agents would not do this.

    It has been revealed that he reported the sighting to the FBI, then learned that the agents, who were headed out of state, had just stopped by to try to vote themselves. The episode generated a flurry of news coverage.

    “Given the negative media coverage regarding federal agents at the polls, it highlights pretty bad judgment that they demonstrated up in their official vehicles,” Earley said.

    It’s against the law for federal law enforcement to be near polling places.

    It has been revealed that nick Brown, Washington’s attorney general, leads a group of Democratic state officials and voting rights advocates who have been planning how to respond if, indeed, there is real federal interference. The group has “war-gamed” how to react if government agents attempt to commandeer voting equipment or ballots.

    “We’ve seen the tension and chaos that’s in the air,” Brown remarked. He called the federal government “the biggest challenge to smooth elections right now, which is not the way it’s supposed to be.”.

    A DOJ spokesperson remarked “the best preparation for any election official is following federal law.”.

    In a recent development, it’s routine for DOJ monitors to watch over polling places, and the agency has assured states that, in the midterms, its observers will follow the law and not interfere with voting or election administration. Still, state officials remain concerned. During Wyoming’s primary election, poll workers noted they felt uneasy when DOJ monitors asked about their training and to inspect voting systems. The state’s governor criticized these actions as “a bit aggressive” and “irregular.”.

    According to recent reports, the Trump administration’s multipronged effort targeting alleged noncitizen voters has already led to eligible voters being improperly removed from the rolls. Voting rights groups fear this will block some U.S. citizens from being able to vote when they show up on Tuesday.

    Federal officials have made clear they plan to go after anyone they think is committing voter fraud.

    It has been revealed that on the first day of early voting in Texas, Aaron Reitz, the U.S. attorney for the Southern District of Texas, posted a YouTube video announcing his intentions. “If you violate federal election law,” he warned, “I will hunt you down and prosecute you.”.

    Sources indicate that this threat came days after the DOJ sued California, seeking to block the state from counting mail ballots from more than 20,000 voters it claims are “likely” noncitizens. The administration had obtained the state’s public voter rolls, which the DHS had blended with its own immigration information and third-party data.

    In a court filing, California called the claim that there are 20,000 noncitizens on its voter rolls “specious.” Los Angeles County analyzed a sampling of the likely noncitizen voters that the federal government claimed were registered there. Many weren’t registered in the county or had never voted, the analysis showed. Some remarked on their voter registration forms that they were born in the United States.

    Asked about the case, the DOJ told ProPublica, “Federal law prohibits noncitizens from voting in federal elections, and the Department has a duty to enforce it.”.

    Industry observers note that A federal judge has rejected the DOJ’s motion for an emergency order that would have barred California from counting the 20,000 voters’ ballots. (A federal appeals panel later backed that decision.) On Thursday, the administration sent grand jury subpoenas to California officials demanding records about their response to allegations of noncitizens on the state’s rolls. Late Friday, a federal judge issued a restraining order blocking the DOJ’s demands, calling them an “intimidation proposal” that would interfere with legal voting.

    Last week, the DOJ wrote a letter threatening to sue Washington state if officials there refused to review a list of 400 voters it believes to be noncitizens within 24 hours. U.S. Attorney General Todd Blanche told reporters late last month that the department was considering additional actions, saying there were “a number of states that we’re looking at.”.

    Recent findings suggest that in a letter responding to the DOJ, Washington Secretary of State Steve Hobbs called the government list of 400 names “not reliable,” saying it included U.S. citizens, people who aren’t registered to vote and duplicate entries. “Time and time again,” Hobbs wrote, “DHS claims about noncitizen voter registration turn out to be greatly exaggerated or false.”.

    Recent findings suggest that sam Trepel is Rule of Law program director at States United Democracy Center and a former attorney for the DOJ’s Civil Rights Division. She mentioned the agency’s actions involving California and Washington were a “disturbing use of prosecutorial authority.”.

    Trepel worries that the DOJ may try to seize ballots cast by voters identified as likely noncitizens, before or after the election, which would “put their votes at risk and undermine trust more broadly.”.

    Voting rights advocates also worry that the government’s efforts to target noncitizen voters could frighten eligible voters to the point that they won’t show up.

    A federal judge recently put limits on a multistate effort by the DHS to go door-to-door in search of suspected noncitizen voters, at least through Election Day, saying it was illegally intimidating legal voters.

    “A voter could say, ‘Well, maybe I don’t want to put myself on the target list here, maybe I won’t register, or maybe I won’t vote,’” mentioned David Janovsky, acting director of The Constitution Project at the watchdog group Project on Government Oversight.

    States often change laws and rules related to voting.

    Since 2024, Republican-led states have taken a number of steps that experts say will make it more difficult for some of their residents to cast ballots and have them count.

    According to recent reports, A North Carolina law, for example, requires voters to provide proof of identification when sending mail-in ballots. Under new rules, ballots now come with two envelopes, both of which must be sealed. Ballot rejections have skyrocketed, Democracy Docket reported, because voters aren’t sealing the inner envelope.

    Texas and other states have cut back on the number and location of polling places, especially in areas favoring Democrats. In hotly contested Tarrant County, which includes Fort Worth, the number of polling sites was slashed by almost a third. This could increase the risk of long lines and voter confusion on Election Day.

    It has been revealed that voting rights groups such as the Texas Civil Rights Project are tracking two issues involving the state’s voter registration systems. A software error at the Texas Department of Public Safety stopped several hundred thousand new voter registrations from being forwarded to local election officials, preventing them from being added to the rolls. A separate state system for updating registration information wasn’t processing changes for several weeks, leading to more backlogs. Counties say they’ve been able to address these problems.

    Every election features some issues with voting equipment.

    So far, there have been isolated complaints involving touch-screen voting machines — including one from Dolly Parton’s sister in Tennessee — spawning fears that machines have been “rigged” to switch votes.

    According to recent reports, ES&S, the company that makes the machines garnering the complaints, told ProPublica that the company hadn’t received widespread reports. Election experts say occasional problems with touch-screen machines don’t signify tampering or manipulation. Any attempt to tamper with programming would surface during testing by election officials and be corrected, they mentioned.

    Incidents in the run-up to the midterms have ratcheted up election officials’ concerns about the potential for both cyber and physical attacks.

    According to recent reports, last month, officials in several states, including Arizona, received envelopes with an unknown white powder. Arizona eventually deemed the material nontoxic, but Secretary of State Adrian Fontes noted “the fear it caused was real.”.

    Sources indicate that in 2024, false bomb threats, thought to be from foreign actors, caused widespread evacuations of vote-counting sites across the country. The disruptions were brief, however, in part because a message board funded by the federal Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, or CISA, alerted election officials that the FBI had deemed the threats not credible.

    In a recent development, trump, however, has dismantled CISA since retaking the presidency, leaving states and local election officials to grapple with both physical and cyber threats on their own. Election nonprofits have stepped up to try to fill the gap, and states, with CISA’s help, have enhanced their own cyber defenses.

    Derek Tisler, counsel and manager for the elections and government program at the Brennan Center for Justice, noted the federal government’s absence has weakened the defenses.

    “States acting on their own just do not have the same power,” he stated.

    Election lawyers fear that actions by the Trump administration in the run-up to the midterms suggest the government will aggressively pursue postelection challenges if the results are not to the president’s liking.

    Late last month, the DOJ sued Alaska, seeking to block the state from certifying the result of its Senate race if the Republican incumbent doesn’t win. A federal judge threw out that lawsuit on Sunday, but the administration is expected to appeal.

    Trump has noted he personally ordered the lawsuit to be filed. It claims the system is unfairly rigged against Sen. Dan Sullivan, because another Alaska man named Dan Sullivan also qualified for the general election ballot. The New York Times reported last week that campaign aides to Democratic Senate nominee Mary Peltola orchestrated the candidacy of the second Dan Sullivan after a monthslong, statewide search to recruit someone with the same name.

    Nonetheless, the DOJ’s case is unusual, both because federal law prohibits the government from interfering with an active election and because challenges typically come after voting is complete. Postelection challenges are most often brought by losing candidates in state courts.

    “This is using the federal government to interfere with our election process in a way that I think is pretty troubling on multiple levels,” said Brown, the Washington attorney general.

    In response to ProPublica’s questions, the DOJ pointed to Blanche’s statement about the lawsuit on social media, which stated the agency “does not seek to stop any ballot from being cast or to stop the certification of Alaska’s election.” (The lawsuit calls it “vital” that the state not certify “any election result that may be impacted by voter confusion” and asks the judge to prevent Alaska from doing this.).

    Recent findings suggest that some election lawyers have suggested that if the GOP suffers significant losses, Trump could try to pressure Republicans in Congress to block fresh members from being seated. Several lawyers, including Derek Muller, a law professor at the University of Notre Dame, say that the incoming Democratic majority would be able to fend off such an effort; courts, too, are likely to stymie it, though it might cause a short delay, according to Muller.

    Brown noted he and other attorneys general are also planning how to respond if local election officials or boards refuse to certify election results, based on their own claims of fraud or claims by the administration.

    “I worry tremendously about what they might do,” Brown said.

    17 major federal agencies flagged over cybersecurity gaps as watchdog warns of increased attack risk

    📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (710 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Foxnews

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Wright and Turner examine growing concerns over the federal government's cybersecurity preparedness, potential vulnerabilities across government agencies and the risks posed by increasingly sophisticated cyber threats.
    • A sweeping federal watchdog report found that 17 of 22 major civilian agencies failed to fully address key cybersecurity planning guidance, warning that the shortcomings could leave government systems more vulnerable to cyberattacks and operational disruptions.
    • The Government Accountability Office (GAO) released its findings this week, identifying gaps at the Departments of Homeland Security (DHS), Justice (DOJ), State, Treasury and Health and Human Services (HHS), among others.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Wright and Turner examine growing concerns over the federal government's cybersecurity preparedness, potential vulnerabilities across government agencies and the risks posed by increasingly sophisticated cyber threats.

    A sweeping federal watchdog report found that 17 of 22 major civilian agencies failed to fully address key cybersecurity planning guidance, warning that the shortcomings could leave government systems more vulnerable to cyberattacks and operational disruptions.

    The Government Accountability Office (GAO) released its findings this week, identifying gaps at the Departments of Homeland Security (DHS), Justice (DOJ), State, Treasury and Health and Human Services (HHS), among others.

    The report examined whether agencies had incorporated selected federal guidance into their plans for implementing zero trust architecture, a cybersecurity approach requiring users, devices and systems to be verified before accessing protected networks.

    RETIRED FBI AGENT WARNS NCIC BREACH COULD THREATEN POLICE SAFETY DURING TRAFFIC STOPS.

    The GAO report discovered that 17 of 22 federal agencies did not meet cybersecurity planning standards. (Getty Images).

    Only five of the 22 agencies fully addressed the selected guidance as of August 2026, prompting GAO to issue 40 recommendations to the remaining 17.

    "Agencies would therefore be at increased risk of cyberattacks that could interrupt operations or otherwise compromise agency resources," GAO warned.

    HHS received six recommendations, the most of any agency reviewed, after investigators found that it lacked a documented enterprise-wide zero trust implementation strategy covering all its information systems.

    Although individual divisions were pursuing cybersecurity improvements, GAO warned that the absence of a unified strategy could prevent department leadership from maintaining a coherent view of its security modernization efforts.

    HHS agreed with the recommendations and noted it planned to develop an actionable department-wide strategy by the second quarter of fiscal year 2027.

    CHINESE HACKERS TARGET NASA AND KEY US AGENCIES, DOJ ALLEGES.

    The Department of Commerce received four recommendations after investigators identified shortcomings in its cybersecurity planning documentation.

    Commerce officials told GAO that staffing losses had significantly constrained the department's zero trust working group, limiting its ability to coordinate improvements and maintain comprehensive documentation.

    At DHS, investigators found that the department had not fully documented cybersecurity maturity levels across all its high-value assets and high-impact systems. Officials attributed the incomplete assessments partly to lengthy government shutdowns during the preceding fiscal year.

    DHS INVESTIGATES MASSIVE DATA BREACH EXPOSING 40,000 EMPLOYEES, INCLUDING ICE AND BORDER PATROL AGENTS.

    Sources indicate that GAO attributed many of the incomplete reports to the prior fiscal year's government shutdown. (iStock).

    DOJ similarly cited resource constraints for incomplete assessments of critical systems, while State and Treasury were among the agencies that had only partially documented cybersecurity maturity levels.

    GAO warned that incomplete assessments could leave agency leadership without the visibility necessary to determine where additional cybersecurity resources are needed.

    Investigators also found that 11 agencies had only partially documented procedures for identifying actors within their IT environments, including certain non-person entities such as software applications and service accounts.

    The watchdog warned that incomplete identification procedures could hinder efforts to ensure only authorized customers and systems access government resources.

    TRUMP’S NATIONAL CYBER DIRECTOR SEAN CAIRNCROSS FIRED AMID WIDESPREAD TECH OUTAGES.

    According to recent reports, the report found that 11 agencies had only partially documented cybersecurity procedures. (Thomas Trutschel/Photothek via Getty Images).

    The findings come years after the Biden administration directed federal agencies to adopt zero trust cybersecurity principles through a 2021 executive order, followed by additional guidance in 2022 and 2024. Despite those directives, GAO found that 17 of 22 agencies still had not fully addressed selected cybersecurity planning requirements and guidance as of August 2026.

    Thirteen agencies agreed with GAO's 40 recommendations, while four neither agreed nor disagreed. The Nuclear Regulatory Commission, one of the four, provided documentation demonstrating that it had already addressed both recommendations, which GAO verified.

    CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP.

    Fox News Digital reached out to the White House and all 17 agencies identified in the report for comment.

    "Absent a full implementation of ZTA requirements and guidance, agencies will lack an appropriate roadmap to fully incorporate and maintain an effective zero trust architecture," GAO concluded.

    Jasmine Baehr is a breaking news writer for Fox News Digital, where she covers politics, the military, legal debates surrounding life and family policy, as well as faith and culture.

    Black voters could sway the midterms in surprising places

    📅 03 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1262 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Salon

    ⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Industry observers note that loss aversion is a phenomenon in psychology and behavioral economics.
    • That’s what appears to be happening right now with Black voters.
    • It has been revealed that in the Trump era, Republicans have become experienced at taking rights away from the American people.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Industry observers note that loss aversion is a phenomenon in psychology and behavioral economics. Defined simply, it means that the pain experienced from a loss is felt twice as much as winning. In politics, that intensity manifests itself in motivation. If you take something away from people, they are going to feel it more acutely than promising them something, and the theft produces a backlash.

    That’s what appears to be happening right now with Black voters. Across the country, they have been lining up to vote early, presumably against Donald Trump and the Republican Party’s MAGA agenda, in astonishing numbers, particularly in the South. That this comes only six months after the Supreme Court gutted the Voting Rights Act in Louisiana v. Callais should not come as a surprise.

    It has been revealed that in the Trump era, Republicans have become experienced at taking rights away from the American people. For women, it was the roll back of their constitutional rights when the Supreme Court overturned Roe v. Wade in 2022, sparking a backlash in that year’s midterm elections. Since Trump returned to office in January 2025, immigrants have come under assault from a xenophobic administration intent on carrying out mass deportations via masked, secret police rampaging through neighborhoods. The LGBTQ+ community, and trans people in particular, have seen their rights stripped away.

    To many Black Americans, the GOP’s agenda and behavior will not have come as a surprise. After all, it’s been at the core of their history going back to before the country’s founding.

    These policies have come as a shock to some Americans who never thought Trump would go there, and they have also opened the eyes of others to the cruelty at the heart of MAGA, overseen by the highest court of the land. But to many Black Americans, the GOP’s agenda and behavior will not have come as a surprise. After all, it’s been at the core of their history going back to before the country’s founding.

    According to recent reports, black Americans know what it means to have their civil rights taken away from them. They understand fully the fear of being targeted by brutal, marauding gangs of armed men. In the decade following the Civil War and the passage of the 14th and 15th Amendments, Black people began to participate fully in civil society. Mississippi elected two Black U.S. senators and a lieutenant governor, and former slaves and their offspring enjoyed freedom of speech, movement and opportunity. But the white members of Southern society would not let that stand, and as soon as the federal government withdrew its troops, they stepped in with legal and social barriers to deny Black Americans their rights, this time backed by vigilante and state violence that became Jim and Jane Crow.

    Almost a century had passed by the time Lyndon Johnson signed the Civil Rights Act in 1964 and the Voting Rights Act in 1965, a period characterized by subjugation and violence by the white majority. But Black America kept fighting, against all odds, until they won.

    This year, we have seen yet another attempt by reactionary politicians and judges to turn back the clock. After the Callais decision, several Southern states reverted immediately to form and radically redrew their congressional districts to favor the white majority, making it much more difficult for voters to elect a Black federal and state representatives.

    They may come to regret that decision. This isn’t 1955 (or 1855) anymore, as much as Donald Trump would like to make it so, and the Black community is once again mobilizing. According to experts, early voting data is showing something unexpected: The vote is being driven by young voters rather than just those who went through the earlier battles. It’s muscle memory for the Black community.

    It has been revealed that after 2024, when Trump won a surprising 15% of the Black vote — nearly doubling his share of 8% in the 2020 election — Republicans thought they were defying history to make great inroads within the community. Then, incredibly, the administration began attacking Black America. The result is what some politicos are calling a “Blacklash,” and it could very well be decisive in some places where nobody expected the Democrats to do well. And even if it doesn’t result in flipping seats, it’s a shot across the bow.

    In Mississippi, prosecutor and former judge Scott Colom, who is Black, is running an excellent race against Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith, the GOP incumbent. Colom has made some very clever advertisements which have garnered a lot of national attention, but Republicans and Democrats alike had largely ignored the race until just a couple of months ago. Polling has tightened, and the GOP has dispatched an influx of luminaries, including Trump himself. For the first time in years, Democrats from Bill Clinton to Kamala Harris, along with a long line of senators, have descended on the state to support Colom. Former President Barack Obama even cut an ad for him. Mississippi has the largest population of Black voters of any state in the country. If Colum gets a massive Black turnout with just enough disaffected whites, he could win.

    According to recent reports, louisiana, after giving birth to the case that saw the Supreme Court’s conservative majority gut the Voting Rights Act, has been winnowed down to one majority Black district in a state that is one-third African-American. But there has been a surge in Black participation akin to what is seen in presidential years, which could prove decisive in a race for Louisiana’s open Senate seat that has been a sleeper until the last couple of weeks. According to a recent poll, Republican Julia Letlow and Democrat Jamie Davis are tied. Among voters who have already cast their ballot, Davis — who is Black — holds a six-point advantage, and 34% of early votes have been cast by Black Louisianans.

    We need your help to stay independent.

    Then there’s South Carolina, which has seen Trump make three desperate appearances to shore up Darline Graham’s torpid campaign. The endangered incumbent, foisted upon South Carolina Republicans by the president himself following the sudden death of her brother, Sen. Lindsey Graham, is not getting the job done. As numbers cruncher Nate Silver pointed out, a recent Upcoming York Times poll showing the race essentially tied is not an outlier; she is in deep trouble. As of late October, the Times reports, “Black voters accounted for around 28 percent of early votes, while making up around 20 percent of the overall electorate in recent cycles. The trend is not unlike what we’re seeing in Georgia and North Carolina thus far.” If that holds true through Election Day, we could see the biggest upset of the whole campaign, largely due to Black South Carolinians saying “Enough is enough.”.

    According to recent reports, in a few short hours, all the ads, mailers, signs and rallies will mercifully come to an end. I am cautiously optimistic, but like many, I’ll never celebrate prematurely again. There is good reason, though, to feel more positive than we have in a long time. Trump and his acolytes have overreached. Opting for the major tech credo of “move fast and break things,” they vastly overestimated their abilities — and the American people’s tolerance.

    Industry observers note that they have also aroused a group of Americans who know what it is to lose their rights and privileges. With all that history and so many battles, Black Americans have shown what it takes to never give up.

    • Dan McLaughlin is a senior writer at National Review Online and a fellow at National Review Institute.

    In a recent development, populism, for all of its faults, can be a powerful force in politics when it is rising. While populist agendas can come in many different varieties, they are all propelled by a broad sense that the people — or more properly, The People — are being held back by some elite force, whether that be Massive Business or an insular political establishment or something darker. If only we can overcome the enemy, we are told, we will sweep to victory on the broad, sunny uplands.

    As I’ve noted before, the very nature of populism is that it has to redefine The People to include something less than all the people when it inevitably encounters the reality that its premises are not universally shared. And so it goes from there, because populism always sooner or later must decide to cling to its narratives when forced to choose between them and empirical reality:.

    Dan McLaughlin is a senior writer at National Review Online and a fellow at National Review Institute.

    On “Populism Isn’t Built for Setbacks”.

    #134002. Tom Petty and The Who box sets reveal two sides of rock history

    📅 03 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 16m • 📚 Deep Dive (3189 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Salon ↗ Open Full Page

    Tom Petty and The Who box sets reveal two sides of rock history

    📅 03 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 16 min read (3189 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Salon

    ⏱️ ~16 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Sources indicate that two great box sets being released for the holiday season from Tom Petty & the Heartbreakers and The Who showcase different approaches to exploring an artist’s back catalog with strong results on both sides.
    • “It’s not Tom Petty good.” That’s how Adria Petty described the standards against which decisions were made about what to include and not to include in the outtakes record.
    • In the case of the Petty box set, the records at its heart are the newly mixed and remastered editions of the first two albums: the eponymous first release and record number two, “You’re Gonna Get It!” Then there’s “Live from the Record Plant,” originally broadcast on KSAN-FM in 1977, a DVD of the band’s appearance on the BBC’s “Old Grey Whistle Test,” and finally (and most importantly for this release) a disc of unheard tracks: “No Sleep Til L.A.” and “The Cut Out Bin.” (On the LP edition of the box, the latter two are separate albums, but on the CD-only version, the two are consolidated.).
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Sources indicate that two great box sets being released for the holiday season from Tom Petty & the Heartbreakers and The Who showcase different approaches to exploring an artist’s back catalog with strong results on both sides. “Origins 1971-1978” chronicles not just the Heartbreakers’ first two albums but also documents the journey that brought them there, while “The Who By Numbers 50th Anniversary Edition” documents the band’s seventh album in a more traditional box set presentation. Both of the releases successfully accomplish their goals and deliver a worthwhile experience for interested listeners, but follow different paths to reach their respective sonic destinations.

    “It’s not Tom Petty good.” That’s how Adria Petty described the standards against which decisions were made about what to include and not to include in the outtakes record. “Could this be any band? If so, it’s not in there . . . it’s gotta be something that really adds to the canon or we’re just detracting from the canon.”.

    In the case of the Petty box set, the records at its heart are the newly mixed and remastered editions of the first two albums: the eponymous first release and record number two, “You’re Gonna Get It!” Then there’s “Live from the Record Plant,” originally broadcast on KSAN-FM in 1977, a DVD of the band’s appearance on the BBC’s “Old Grey Whistle Test,” and finally (and most importantly for this release) a disc of unheard tracks: “No Sleep Til L.A.” and “The Cut Out Bin.” (On the LP edition of the box, the latter two are separate albums, but on the CD-only version, the two are consolidated.).

    Industry observers note that rounding out the set is a Blu-Ray with hi-res stereo, Dolby Atmos and 5.1 immersive mixes, and importantly, a full-color 46-page “fanzine” called “Heart Attack” that serves as the liner notes for this box, with photographs, essays, interviews and commentary from members of the surviving Heartbreakers. There are other editions with additional advanced artifacts like posters or simulated Polaroids — my favorite is probably the “Punk to Fresh Wave” trading cards — but if you’re in the target market for those kinds of fun treats, you’ve probably already ordered your copy.

    What’s notable about the unreleased music featured on “No Sleep Til L.A.” and “The Cut Out Bin” is that it isn’t just a simple compilation of demos and rough takes in a logical order of some kind, but instead is deliberately curated into the shape of an album. It’s intended to convey the journey Petty and the band took to get to the place where they’re going into the studio to record that first record, capturing tracks from the Mudcrutch era (Petty’s pre-Heartbreakers band that also featured future Heartbreakers Mike Campbell and Benmont Tench) as early as 1971 and then as the Heartbreakers in their early days, learning to work in the studio in L.A. and in Tulsa, where their label Shelter Records sent them to learn how to make a record instead of running the meter on a L.A. studio.

    The outtake record isn’t trying to fabricate something that doesn’t exist or inject fiction into the Heartbreakers legend, but rather, to show you how the band evolved from a bunch of kids in Florida who picked up and went out to L.A. to seek their rock ‘n’ roll fortunes on a wing and a prayer into a band that would end up being inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame. It’s expanding the legacy, not rewriting history.

    “It’s not Tom Petty good.” That’s how Adria Petty, who oversees Petty Legacy, the business concern that’s handling her late father’s catalog, told Salon as she described the standards against which decisions were made about what to include and not to include in the outtakes record. “Could this be any band? If so, it’s not in there . . . it’s gotta be something that really adds to the canon or we’re just detracting from the canon.”.

    Industry observers note that and the collection absolutely burnishes the canon. It’s hard to listen to the selection of music and understand how any music business professional didn’t think this band had serious potential. There’s so many standout tracks: “Parade of Loons,” which opens the record, from the great rock ‘n’ roll tradition of writing a song from the perspective of watching the craziness unfolding around you is borderline fresh wave, but it also isn’t — it’s easy to understand why an industry struggling to understand the new guard needed to figure out where these new guys fit, exactly — and perusing some of the photos included in “Heart Attack” you can extend some grace on that front, because — as Adria Petty laughed, “These are not guys you want to date your daughter, you know?” But as you learn from some of the news clips included in the booklet, Petty did not want to be co-opted into anyone’s movement or limited by any genre.

    “You’re Gonna Learn” is reggae-influenced at a time when that wasn’t a widely known, let alone embraced, genre in American rock, and they manage to pull it off without embarrassing themselves. “Up In Mississippi Tonight” could be an outtake from “Exile on Main Street.” There are also a couple of earnest and successful Dylan homages: “Wild Eyes” and “I Can’t Fight It.” If you’re going to borrow, borrow from the best (and from a guy you’re going to be on the road backing in 10 years).

    Industry observers note that then there’s “Unheard Kind of Hero.” This is a song that Heartbreakers keyboardist Benmont Tench had previously mentioned as a song he saw the band perform before he was in it, and how he was astounded that a band in Gainesville, Florida, was writing original material like that. In “Heart Attack,” Tench offers, “I was following Mudcrutch around because they were so good, and they played a lot of really cool covers and they played some stuff of their own,” he remembers. And when he heard “Hero,” he asked a friend working for the band who sang it originally. When he was told it was an original, his reaction was, “OK, good lord. Because if you listen to that, whether he was 17 or 19 when he wrote it, the storytelling in it is the beginning.”.

    The box set is configured to bring the listener into the story, opening with the outtakes before taking you to the officially released albums, then live radio show and then, finally, the 1977 “Old Grey Whistle Test” performance. But I’d like to make the case that you should begin with the OGWT performance because it is utterly electrifying. Anglophiles are already familiar, but in case you’re not, the “Old Grey Whistle Test” is a legendary BBC music program that was the opposite to “Top of the Pops” in that its focus was on albums as opposed to hit singles. But this isn’t an OGWT where a band plays a couple of songs; this was one of their special editions where the band gets the full show. So this is a 40-minute performance by a band that was already famous and well-liked in the U.K., a status they were still fighting to achieve back home.

    They’re dressed in black (Benmont Tench rocking a red shirt underneath his suit jacket), Petty looking more like a gunslinger, Ray-Ban aviators and studded guitar strap, Stan Lynch singing harmony vocals over Petty’s shoulder, Mike Campbell dropping guitar riffs and solos without breaking a sweat, Ron Blair sharing the center mic for harmony vocals but otherwise staying low-key back against the drum riser. It’s a time machine back to 1977, with camera work more evolved than we’re used to seeing because it was a TV show about music, not a variety show that featured a band. The colors are a little over-saturated, but people who are used to watching archival rock ‘n’ roll clips won’t be phased. The most jarring element is whenever the camera cuts to the audience, who look like they’d rather be anywhere else. A U.K. source shared that this was because this wasn’t an audience of Tom Petty fans but rather random people who’d put in for tickets and wouldn’t have been encouraged to be enthusiastic. Petty gets his revenge, though, at the last number. (No spoilers!).

    It has been revealed that the Who box sets are intended to be complete documents of individual records. So there’s the disc of the remastered album (which sounds fantastic), then the initial Townshend demos.

    It has been revealed that “The Who By Numbers” was released in 1975, but this is still being declared a 50th anniversary artifact. It features 92 unreleased audio tracks, a recording of the band live in Swansea in 1976, the requisite Atmos and stereo mixes, and a video of the full concert of The Who at the Silverdome in Pontiac, Michigan, in 1975.

    Also included is what has become a trademark for the band’s reissue sets, a gorgeous full-color 100-page book of liner notes, interviews, lyrics, photographs and other assorted documentation. Even if you buy the CD box, you’re still getting the full-sized book because they put the CDs into an album-sized enclosure. The archivist this time is Andy Neill, one of the two names you want to see behind a Who reissue.

    The Who box sets are intended to be complete documents of individual records. So there’s the disc of the remastered album (which sounds fantastic), then the initial Townshend demos. Townshend was approaching 30 when he began work on the songs for “By Numbers,” and he was in the middle of a number of personal dilemmas, as well as struggling with his and the band’s place within rock ‘n’ roll: “I felt detached from my own songs,” he confesses. He also rued the fact that he felt he owed his best material to the band, instead of being able to pursue more of a solo career, which all of his bandmates had done. Townshend’s “Who Came First” came out in 1972, but there hadn’t been anything since.

    (Michael Ochs Archives/Getty Images) The Who, 1975.

    The demos are lovely, ethereal sketches, documenting Townshend breathing life into his creations for the first time. There are two demos of “Keep Me Turning,” which didn’t make the cut and we wouldn’t hear until it appeared on “Rough Mix,” the warm and affectionate project he recorded with Ronnie Lane of the Faces two years later. A fun game is to take the Townshend demo of “Slip Kid,” where he’s kind of half-speaking, half-singing, and then compare it to Daltrey’s delivery on the finished version, which is the one song from this record that was built on the original demo. (This is a release that you’ll want the good headphones for.) The highlight is probably “How Many Friends,” which is the heartbreaker on the album; Daltrey’s read of it nails the pathos, but this version makes you wish that Pete maybe hung onto it for himself.

    Recent findings suggest that up next is “Tracking Sessions,” which are initial loose takes with the whole band, but not finished vocals. It’s basically how the band taught themselves the new material, and it includes listings like “Ramport Jam” where they (sans Keith Moon, still making his way back to the U.K. after hanging out in L.A. and working on his solo record) fart around on a variety of instrumentals and a Faces song. This lasted about half an hour, but we’re getting only eight minutes; given the nature of the release, just give the fans the entire unedited mess. Throughout the sessions, you hear the band members making jokes and laughing; you hear Glyn Johns in the control room offering his thoughts; you hear Pete Townshend complaining about not being able to obtain a suitable breakfast. This stuff is gold.

    Whereas the Tom Petty box set is intended to show you how they got to the first two albums, this release is trying to show you why this was the record between “Quadrophenia” and “Who Are You.”.

    Recent findings suggest that there are also lovely early run-throughs of “Imagine A Man” with a solo Townshend on acoustic and Nicky Hopkins on piano, and similarly, “They Are All In Love” (a song that Daltrey did not initially want to sing) is also offered solo Pete. A prototype of “Blue Red and Gray” is here as well, thanks to Glyn Johns’ insistence: “I find that the hardest thing for me to do as a writer is to express optimism, general warmth and a feeling of good will to all men in a song,” Townshend said. “It feels trite and I hate it. That song, ‘I Love Every Minute Of The Day’ . . . is a prime example. Glyn Johns wanted it on the album; I cringed when he picked it. He heard it on a cassette and said, ‘What’s that?’ I said, ‘Nothing.’ He said, ‘No. Play it.’ I said, ‘Really, it’s nothing. Just me playing a ukulele.’ But he insisted on doing it. I said, ‘What? That fu*king thing. Here’s me, wanting to commit suicide, and you’re going to put that thing on the record’.”.

    Disc 4 is billed “Early Mixes & Guide Vocals” and is by nature more structured than the Tracking Sessions. The songs are taking shape now. Entwistle offers his approach to his “Success Story,” Pete sings the lead on “However Much I Booze,” there’s a version of “Squeezebox” that the liner notes state is “accented by tambourine” but sounds like the cowbell on the “SNL” “Don’t Fear The Reaper” sketch, and “Dreaming From The Waist” is a fantastic illustration of why Pete Townshend needed Roger Daltrey to sing most of his songs.

    As a way to track the evolution of the song from start to finish, the inclusion of all of these different versions is an established and useful presentation device, but given their formative nature, it’s not likely that you’re going to go back to them with regularity. But that’s not why this record exists. Whereas the Tom Petty box set is intended to show you how they got to the first two albums, this release is trying to show you why this was the record between “Quadrophenia” and “Who Are You.”.

    It has been revealed that but it’s probably more accurate to state that “The Who By Numbers” was the record between the “Tommy” movie and “Who Are You,” which isn’t a small distinction; the “Tommy” movie made the band into a larger and different flavor of rock star, one that brought in the girls because of shirtless golden god Daltrey and delivered your average punters who might not have found their way past the tunes they’d heard on the radio. And it’s not unimportant to note that the “Tommy” movie brought the band the kind of money they hadn’t yet seen.

    Recent findings suggest that that’s part of the cri de coeur you hear on “By Numbers.” It’s by no means the main thread, but it absolutely underpins Townshend’s personal anxieties. He’s annoyed that his bandmates are off doing their own thing. He’s perturbed that he doesn’t have the time or material to make another solo record because he has to offer his best songs to The Who (and conversely, it’s kind of hilarious that he then seems panicked when he presented Daltrey with the songs he’d written for the record and ended up shocked that Rog picked “the more personal ones”.) NOTE: Daltrey is not responsible for the abomination that is “Squeeze Box,” that we have to blame on Ronnie Lane, who was enchanted by it.

    Sources indicate that the Swansea show from 1976 here isn’t complete, but it is Keith Moon’s last proper show before a U.K. audience. (It was recorded with the intention of being released as a live album, and one of the original tapes went missing at some point in the 1990s, which is why the first two songs are missing.) “My Wife” will sound familiar to anyone who owns the “Maximum RnB” box set, “Squeezebox” is palatable because of Townshend’s giant power chords, “I’m Free” (introduced by Moon, who dedicates it to the occupants of the prison across the street from the venue) sounds more like the version from the “Tommy” soundtrack, and there’s a hilarious comedic bit over “Bellboy.”.

    We need your help to stay independent.

    In a recent development, but it’s the last live artifact here that’s a truly delightful surprise. It’s on the last disc with the Atmos remixes, and at first I feared it would be poor-quality footage added simply because it existed. But it’s far, far better than that. It is the complete show from the Pontiac Silverdome in December of 1975, cleaned up and remastered. This show set the record for the largest ever indoor rock concert attendance of 76,896, which would be broken by Led Zeppelin in the same place two years later. Because of the size of both the venue and the crowd, a large screen was set up to project closed-circuit video, a thing we’d think absolutely nothing of now, but at the time was a revolutionary development.

    It has been revealed that there were four cameras, and they do a more than decent job of capturing the action but don’t expect any fancy camerawork or closeups of guitar solos. The sound is in mono — as the liner notes point out, “the sound was captured via a direct line mono feed from the PA — no attempt was made to professionally record the concert for synching purposes.” Part of the “Join Together” / “Road Runner” / “My Generation” medley ended up in “The Kids Are Alright,” but this is the first official release of this footage.

    You know what? The sound quality is more than adequate, and where it falls down the electricity coming off of that stage in this performance makes up for a multitude of sins. Roger is in Woodstock buckskin fringe, and even this primitive setup can capture that those trousers were, shall we say, form-fitting. (Wait for “Magic Bus,” which swings so much harder and better than it did later.) Daltrey introduces the “Tommy” portion by noting, “This is how we used to do it,” and then the band proceeds to light the stage on fire. The band seems perplexed and concerned about the size of the crowd, with both Roger and Pete each taking turns to ask the crowd to take a few steps back.

    Industry observers note that this Silverdome footage is absolutely a text, and even this rudimentary capture that was meant to make sure the 76,896th guy in the back could see something is still full of electricity and life. If you were lucky enough to see the band with Keith Moon in those days, you’ll remember, and if you weren’t, this at least brings some of that fairy dust into your life and your house. Put it on, turn it all the way up, and enjoy it without 76,896 people stepping on your feet.

    from music columnist Caryn Rose.

    💡 Key Takeaways

    • LaMonica McIver, D-N.J., faced a setback Thursday in her effort to ditch charges tied to a scuffle during an oversight visit at an immigration detention facility last year, as a federal appeals court declined to reconsider its decision to let the case move forward.
    • It has been revealed that the decision by the U.S.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Sources indicate that rep. LaMonica McIver, D-N.J., is seen on Capitol Hill last December. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call).

    Rep. LaMonica McIver, D-N.J., faced a setback Thursday in her effort to ditch charges tied to a scuffle during an oversight visit at an immigration detention facility last year, as a federal appeals court declined to reconsider its decision to let the case move forward.

    It has been revealed that the decision by the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 3rd Circuit leaves in place a 2-1 opinion from August which held that McIver was not immune from the charges, which stemmed from a confrontation between visiting members of Congress and federal agents while at the Delaney Hall facility in Newark. McIver has challenged the charges, arguing that her visit fell under the “speech or debate” immunity she has as a member of Congress because she was there to inspect detention conditions.

    Industry observers note that in a statement McIver mentioned she and her attorneys were looking at “every possible option” in response to the appeals court ruling. Her statement invoked the Trump administration’s threats to treat oversight efforts as criminal conduct and said “we are all one step closer to a world in which the president of the United States can try to imprison people simply because he does not like what they stand for.”.

    According to recent reports, “Donald Trump continues to send warning shots to Democrats in Congress and in all levels of power — but their case against me right now, in broad daylight, goes well beyond a warning. Because of a weaponized Department of Justice and because I dared to do my job and conduct oversight of ICE, I am facing 17 years in prison,” McIver mentioned in her statement.

    Following Thursday’s decision on rehearing, McIver could next ask the Supreme Court to weigh in on the case.

    The August majority opinion from Judge Cindy Chung, which Thursday’s decision leaves in place, said that two of the three charges against McIver did not fall under the immunity, which is limited to legislative acts. The majority sent the third charge back to the lower court for another ruling.

    “We have considered the ‘nature’ of the charged conduct and concluded it is unambiguously non-legislative,” the judge wrote.

    It has been revealed that separately, Judge Thomas Ambro partially dissented to offer a different approach to the case. Ambro would have required the trial judge to more closely examine the exact conduct McIver was charged with, as well as to examine whether the Trump administration targeted her because of her political views.

    “I would allow her discovery into the truth of the matter — not only for her own sake but to safeguard the independence of our legislative bodies,” Ambro wrote.

    It has been revealed that ambro did not vote on whether the full 3rd Circuit should rehear the case. Three judges voted to have the full 3rd Circuit hear McIver’s case, and Judge Emil Bove, a former Trump administration official and former personal attorney for the president, did not participate in the vote.

    The criminal case started shortly after the Delaney Hall visit in May 2025, as prosecutors alleged that McIver assaulted federal agents during a scuffle around Newark Mayor Ras Baraka. Officials arrested Baraka that day and charged him with trespassing, but later dropped those charges.

    Recent findings suggest that court filings in the case alleged that McIver struck agents during the confrontation. McIver has argued that she was effectively being charged for doing her job and federal agents were interfering with her attempts to inspect the facility.

    It has been revealed that earlier this year, Judge Jamel K. Semper of the U.S. District Court for the District of New Jersey disagreed and ruled that the case could move forward.

    Will the midterms live up to the hype? 6 key stories we’re watching

    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Recent findings suggest that across the country, voters are making their way to the polls in the climax of a vitriolic midterm election cycle set against the backdrop of an electorate souring on Donald Trump and Republicans.
    • Each election is billed as being consequential; this one lives up to the hype.
    • Industry observers note that A tsunami, a trickle — or something in the middle?
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Recent findings suggest that across the country, voters are making their way to the polls in the climax of a vitriolic midterm election cycle set against the backdrop of an electorate souring on Donald Trump and Republicans. Inflation is up, consumer confidence is down, gas and diesel prices are through the roof, largely due to the president’s war of choice in Iran. The cruelty of his MAGA agenda has roiled the country and left a bad taste even in the mouths of some of his erstwhile supporters.

    Each election is billed as being consequential; this one lives up to the hype. As we await the results, it’s worth taking note of several questions:.

    Industry observers note that A tsunami, a trickle — or something in the middle? All are possible, but signs are pointing to significant Democratic gains, likely up to 25 seats in the House, as well as a Senate majority. Dr. Abdul El-Sayed looks increasingly likely to win in Michigan, and James Talarico has Democratic hopes up in Texas. Senate races in Maine, Kansas, Iowa and Alaska are in play, and it’s worth keeping an eye on South Carolina, Mississippi and Louisiana as well.

    One sign will come at 6 p.m. when polls close in Kentucky’s 6th Congressional District, where Democrat Zach Dembo is facing off against Republican Ralph Alvarado. Once a Democratic stronghold, the seat went Republican in 2012 and, despite a close call in 2018, has remained in GOP hands since. Although the district has been gerrymandered to favor Republicans, the energy on the ground is with Dembo. If he posts and maintains a healthy lead, look for significant Democratic gains to unfold throughout the night.

    What effect did redistricting have on the GOP’s chances?

    According to recent reports, the midterms will be the first test of the GOP’s redistricting strategy, which saw the party redraw congressional districts in Florida, Texas and other states, partly in response to the gains Trump made with Black and Latino voters in 2024. But polls show those margins have been largely erased as the electorate has turned on the president after nearly two tumultuous years in office, while Democratic legislatures in California and Virginia have imposed their own gerrymanders. According to a Politico poll, the GOP increasingly sees the coalition that returned Trump to office as “crumbling,” and may have gained little or nothing from all this adventurous map-drawing.

    Will progressives be bolstered or chastened?

    It has been revealed that losses — or even narrow wins — by progressive candidates could be used as more evidence by the party’s establishment wing of the need to tack toward the middle ahead of the 2028 presidential election. Larger wins would provide rocket fuel to the movement.

    Sources indicate that the size of the blue wave could well come to be seen as a measure of progressives’ influence and power within the Democratic Party. Losses — or even narrow wins — by progressive candidates could be used as more evidence by the party’s establishment wing of the need to tack toward the middle ahead of the 2028 presidential election. Larger wins — and victories in unexpected places, such as Michigan’s 7th Congressional District where William Lawrence, co-founder of the Sunrise Movement, stands a real chance of unseating incumbent Republican Tom Barrett — would provide rocket fuel to the movement.

    Progressive groups are already on the offensive, getting a head start on spinning tonight’s election results, particularly in anticipation of a narrow El-Sayed win in Michigan. “Expect to hear narrow victories cited as evidence of weak electability,” a Progressive Change Campaign Committee memo obtained by Politico reads. “But a candidate’s first winning margin is not their electoral ceiling.”.

    Will the Haley Stevens drama matter in Michigan?

    Haley Stevens, the Democratic congresswoman who narrowly lost to El-Sayed in Michigan’s Senate primary, has brought the drama in the race’s closing days. As late as Saturday night, she pledged to colleagues and friends that she was backing El-Sayed, only to turn up hours later at a church service with his Republican opponent Mike Rogers, and endorse the former congressman in a video. The cold-dish move has virtually drowned out El-Sayed’s closing message, with Stevens being formally kicked out of the Michigan Democratic Party.

    The question now is if any of it will matter, especially in light of a Fresh York Times/Siena poll taken before Stevens’ move that demonstrated El-Sayed leading Rogers by 11 points. Michigan Republicans seem to think it won’t, telling Politico they wish the congresswoman had crossed the aisle earlier. The nonpartisan Cook Political Report agrees, moving the race in their ratings to “Leans Democratic,” a shift that was already in the works before Stevens detonated her bomb.

    Still, the results in the state’s Democratic primary were far narrower than the polls revealed, with El-Sayed besting Stevens by only 1%, or 14,893 votes.

    Will Elon Musk get his money’s worth?

    The New York Times reported yesterday that the world’s first trillionaire has dropped a staggering $474 million this election cycle, an historic first. The amount has been spread out across a variety of groups, PACs and funds, but it doesn’t include the “dark-money donations” the Times reports he has also made. Most of the $168 million he contributed to the Senate Leadership Fund has served to shore up Ken Paxton, the GOP nominee for Senate in Texas, who is locked in a tight race with Talarico.

    In a recent development, musk has a lot riding on Tuesday’s results. Beyond the simple math of whether he got enough bang for his buck, there is also the concern of what will surely face him in the event of a Democratic congressional majority: investigations.

    According to recent reports, musk has a lot riding on Tuesday’s results. Beyond the simple math of whether he got enough bang for his buck, there is also the issue of what will surely face him in the event of a Democratic congressional majority: investigations. If the blue wave materializes, Musk can expect congressional inquiries of his activities, including his reported interventions in Russia’s war against Ukraine and his leadership of DOGE during the early months of Trump’s second administration.

    It has been revealed that each election brings surprises. Think not one but both of Georgia’s Senate seats going to Democrats in 2020, or Republicans making massive gains in New York two years later.

    This is the year we could hear the echo of Georgia’s 2020 election results in another Southern state. Despite boasting large Black populations, Senate seats in South Carolina, Mississippi and Louisiana have long been out of reach for Democrats. But there is now a path to victory for the party’s candidates in each of those states.

    Industry observers note that in South Carolina, the GOP incumbent Darline Graham, who was appointed to the seat at Donald Trump’s command following the death of her brother, Sen. Lindsey Graham, has proven to be a lackluster candidate, alarming even some Republicans with her performance in debates and on the stump. Democrat Annie Andrews has run a more nimble campaign, and between Graham’s performance and the national state of affairs, she appears to have narrowed the gap.

    We need your help to stay independent.

    It has been revealed that mississippi’s incumbent GOP Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith has also run a lazy campaign, expecting to coast to victory. But the national political environment under Trump, coupled with campaign gaffes, large Black turnout in the aftermath of the Supreme Court’s decision to gut the Voting Rights Act and clever campaigning by Scott Colom, her Democratic opponent, have helped to put the race in play.

    Louisiana is also a wild card. The state, which is one-third African American, has also seen a surge in early voting among Black residents, and according to a recent poll, the race between Republican Julia Letlow and Democrat Jamie Davis, who is Black, is tied.

    In a recent development, polls are not predictive. The political history of these states continues to favor Republicans, but any of them could deliver one of 2026’s electoral surprises. If that happens, it will signal that the blue wave has become a blue tsunami.

    #133999. Elon Musk is using Anakin Skywalker to cope with the midterm forecast

    📅 03 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (694 w)
