    Iran resolution blocked in first war powers vote since midterms

    📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (846 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rollcall

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Tim Kaine, D-Va., seen here at the Capitol on June 17, said additional war powers votes are under discussion for when Democrats control both chambers in the 120th Congress.
    • The Senate rejected a resolution Thursday meant to rebuke President Donald Trump over the Iran war weeks after the midterm elections demonstrated the depth of public anger about the war and its effects on the U.S.
    • In a recent development, senators voted 48-51 against adopting the Iran war powers resolution that the House previously adopted in mid-September that would direct the president to withdraw U.S.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    It has been revealed that sen. Tim Kaine, D-Va., seen here at the Capitol on June 17, said additional war powers votes are under discussion for when Democrats control both chambers in the 120th Congress. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call).

    The Senate rejected a resolution Thursday meant to rebuke President Donald Trump over the Iran war weeks after the midterm elections demonstrated the depth of public anger about the war and its effects on the U.S. economy.

    In a recent development, senators voted 48-51 against adopting the Iran war powers resolution that the House previously adopted in mid-September that would direct the president to withdraw U.S. forces from the war.

    Sources indicate that as they have previously with similar measures, GOP Sens. Susan Collins of Maine, Lisa Murkowski of Alaska and Rand Paul of Kentucky broke with their party to support the resolution, while Democratic Sen. John Fetterman of Pennsylvania broke with his party to oppose it. Departing GOP Sens. Thom Tillis of North Carolina and Bill Cassidy of Louisiana, who have at times voted in support of similar measures, this time voted against the resolution.

    Even if the resolution was adopted in both chambers of Congress, it would be largely symbolic since, as a concurrent resolution, it would not go to the president for his signature.

    But the vote afforded senators the opportunity to register their complaints about the war for the first time since Democrats routed Republicans in the midterm elections.

    It also comes amid a larger debate within the Democratic Party on how best to fulfill their campaign promise of ending the war as they prepare to take control of Congress next year.

    Democrats have become increasingly interested in trying to cut off funding for the war rather than continuing to hold war powers votes. But they are divided on whether to demand an immediate end to funding in the next government funding bill in December or to wait until they take power in January.

    “When we have the gavels, we are contemplating other things, and we're actually contemplating things in connection with the CR discussion,” Sen. Tim Kaine, D-Va., told reporters Thursday in an apparent reference to the debate among Democrats.

    As of Nov. 13, the war has cost at least $48.3 billion, up from $47 billion last month, the nominee to be Navy comptroller, Arthur Miller, told the Senate Armed Services Committee at his confirmation hearing Thursday.

    As with previous estimates, the number Miller cited Thursday includes munitions, equipment replacement costs and operational costs but does not factor in the cost of damage to U.S. bases, which alone is likely to run in the billions.

    Sources indicate that last week, a trio of Senate Democrats unveiled legislation to prohibit funding for offensive military operations in Iran that they stated they intend to introduce as an amendment to the next government funding bill, which Congress will need to pass to avoid a government shutdown after Dec. 11.

    It has been revealed that on Thursday as the Senate voted on the war powers resolution, Sens. Tammy Duckworth, D-Ill., and Kirsten Gillibrand, D-N.Y., two of the sponsors of the proposed amendment, demanded it be included in the next funding bill.

    “We’ve already tried tool after tool to get the president to rein in this conflict. Nine months in, defunding the war is the only way to force Trump to end it,” Duckworth, who vowed to vote against any continuing resolution that doesn’t include the amendment, said at a news conference.

    Sources indicate that sen. Michael Bennet, D-Colo., unveiled his own proposed amendment Thursday to bar any future and previous funding from being used to “support directly or indirectly combat activities by United States personnel in or over Iran, or in Iranian territorial waters” unless specifically authorized by Congress.

    His legislation is modeled off of language Congress passed in 1973 to cut off funding for the Nixon administration’s bombing campaign in Cambodia, Bennet’s office said in a news release.

    According to recent reports, “When we vote on short-term spending in the near future, we can fund the government and end this war. It is what the American people demand, and what they deserve,” Bennet noted in a statement.

    Meanwhile, the House is likely to vote again on a war powers resolution before year’s end.

    “Before the lame duck’s over, I hope to enforce a war powers resolution vote, and it’ll be a chance for Republicans to say whether they did or didn’t get the message on Nov. 3,” Rep. Thomas Massie, R-Ky., said Thursday in a brief interview, referring to the date of the elections.

    Industry observers note that as with previous resolutions, Massie’s would direct the president to remove U.S. military units from hostilities against Iran unless specifically authorized by Congress or needed to defend against an imminent attack.

    Industry observers note that the resolution was filed Nov. 10, and under the 1973 War Powers Resolution, Massie can force a vote 15 calendar days after its introduction.

    Industry observers note that john M. Donnelly and Lauren Green contributed to this report.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Pat Hogan, CEO of CMB Regional Centers, alleges fraud in a $275 million Treasury grant obtained by Crescent Dunes’ former owner and companies linked to Spanish construction giant Cobra.
    • This article is Part 2 of a Fox News Digital exclusive series investigating the Crescent Dunes solar power plant in Nevada.
    • The Trump administration has made fighting fraud and rooting out government waste a top priority, even offering cash rewards to Americans who expose wrongdoing.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Pat Hogan, CEO of CMB Regional Centers, alleges fraud in a $275 million Treasury grant obtained by Crescent Dunes’ former owner and companies linked to Spanish construction giant Cobra.

    This article is Part 2 of a Fox News Digital exclusive series investigating the Crescent Dunes solar power plant in Nevada. You can read Part 1 here.

    The Trump administration has made fighting fraud and rooting out government waste a top priority, even offering cash rewards to Americans who expose wrongdoing.

    Yet investors in a failed Obama-era solar plant are questioning why President Donald Trump's own Justice Department is fighting to squash their fraud lawsuit over a $275 million federal grant — a case they say could recover up to $1 billion for taxpayers.

    The investors allege that Spanish construction giant ACS and companies to tied its former subsidiary Cobra, misled federal officials into approving the grant by claiming the troubled solar plant was ready for use, even though it had suffered major construction problems and was shut down for months following a molten-salt-tank failure.

    The lawsuit centers on the beleaguered Crescent Dunes solar plant, a billion-dollar, government-backed project that began operating in Nevada in 2015 but was later plagued by engineering failures, repeated shutdowns and two bankruptcies before being sold for just $7 million in July.

    HOW A $1B OBAMA-ERA SOLAR PLANT WENT BANKRUPT TWICE, LEAVING TAXPAYERS WITH THE TAB.

    Recent findings suggest that an aerial view of the Crescent Dunes Solar Energy Project near Tonopah, Nevada, shows thousands of mirrors concentrating sunlight onto the central tower in footage published in 2018. The billion-dollar solar plant later went through two bankruptcies before being sold for $7 million in 2026. (ferrantraite/iStock via Getty Images).

    The plant was built around an emerging solar technology that used thousands of mirrors to concentrate sunlight onto a towering receiver, heating molten salt that could be stored and used to generate electricity even after sunset.

    In 2020, a group of private investors who had put $90 million into the project and suffered substantial losses filed a whistleblower lawsuit, alleging the companies had misled the federal government to secure the enormous grant.

    But in November 2024, just two days after Trump's re-election, Biden's Justice Department moved to shut down the lawsuit, arguing that pursuing the case would burden federal agencies.

    WHITE HOUSE ROLLS OUT INTERACTIVE MAP TRACKING BILLIONS IN SUSPECTED FRAUD.

    SolarReserve, ACS Group/Cobra and Banco Santander were original project participants in Crescent Dunes, which received a $737 million Department of Energy loan guarantee and approximately $275.6 million in Treasury grant awards. CMB investors also provided $90 million in private financing. (Fox News).

    DOJ UNVEILS NATIONWIDE TAX FRAUD CRACKDOWN INVOLVING 76 DEFENDANTS, NEARLY $500M IN ALLEGED LOSSES.

    The incoming Trump administration could have reconsidered that position in early 2025. Instead, its Justice Department defended the Biden-era dismissal in an April filing with a federal appeals court.

    In a recent development, CMB, an investment group headed by Pat Hogan, is appealing the dismissal. Hogan is also urging Trump’s Justice Department to ask the court to reopen the case.

    "It makes no sense," Hogan told Fox News Digital in a video interview.

    Hogan remarked he had contacted Trump's Justice Department seeking help reviving the case but had received no commitment.

    "The real problem here is, why isn't the government asking for this?" he noted. "All in all, I would say this has just been a fleecing of the federal government by a foreign entity. And we have the opportunity to fix it, and they're doing nothing.".

    Hogan argues that allowing the lawsuit to proceed could potentially net hundreds of millions of dollars for taxpayers.

    Under the False Claims Act, which CMB used to bring its lawsuit, companies found liable can face damages of up to three times the government's proven losses, plus additional penalties.

    "This could be a billion dollars," Hogan mentioned.

    Tonopah Solar Energy, the plant's former owner and one of the defendants, has rejected CMB's allegations as baseless in court filings. Other companies named in the lawsuit have also backed the Justice Department's effort to dismiss the case.

    Sources indicate that in an April 2026 court filing, Trump's Justice Department defended the Biden administration's decision, making the same argument that continuing the lawsuit would drain government resources and that federal law gave it broad authority to shut down the case. In court filings reviewed by Fox News Digital, neither administration put a dollar figure on the cost of continuing the lawsuit.

    The decision has left Hogan and his investors questioning why the government shut down the case — and what Treasury officials knew about the plant's serious problems when they approved the $275 million grant.

    Sources indicate that pat Hogan, CEO of CMB Regional Centers, whose investors provided $90 million in financing for the Crescent Dunes solar project, is challenging the dismissal of a federal whistleblower lawsuit alleging fraud involving a $275 million Treasury grant. (Provided).

    It has been revealed that the Crescent Dunes solar plant in Tonopah, Nevada, left, received approximately $275.6 million in Treasury grant awards. Private investors allege the plant's former owner and companies involved in its construction fraudulently obtained the funding. The allegations remain disputed, and a federal judge dismissed the whistleblower lawsuit at the Justice Department's request. (Michael Dorgan/Fox News Digital; Daniel Heuer/Bloomberg via Getty Images).

    At the heart of the lawsuit is a dispute over whether Crescent Dunes was properly completed — and whether its owner, Tonopah Solar Energy, was entitled to collect the $275 million Treasury grant.

    The grant was part of a $26 billion program within the Obama administration's broader $90 billion green-energy push, rolled out under the 2009 economic stimulus package to create jobs and turbocharge its green energy agenda.

    Known as Section 1603, the program paid developers about 30% of their qualifying construction costs once their facilities were "placed in service" — meaning ready and available for their intended use. Treasury considered several factors in determining whether a plant met that standard, including whether it had passed critical tests, begun generating electricity and come under its owner's control.

    Crescent Dunes began generating electricity in 2015, but CMB alleges it had produced no more than 32% of its expected output through June 2016.

    Then, in October 2016, a failure involving the plant's hot molten-salt storage tank shut it down for months.

    Sources indicate that A diagram displayed at the Crescent Dunes Solar Energy Project near Tonopah, Nevada, illustrates how thousands of mirrors concentrate sunlight onto a central receiver, heating molten salt that is stored in tanks and used to generate electricity. The diagram bears the Crescent Dunes Solar Energy logo. (Michael Dorgan/Fox News Digital).

    In December, while Crescent Dunes was still shut down, its builder, Cobra Thermosolar Plants, formally handed the plant over to its owner, Tonopah Solar Energy, under an arrangement known as "provisional acceptance.".

    But first, they changed the construction contract to allow the handover despite major defects and unfinished repairs.

    That agreement came just days before the year-end deadline for solar plants to be ready for use to qualify for the Treasury grants.

    In a later court filing, CMB alleged that more than 9,000 defects had been identified and grouped into roughly 500 outstanding construction items, including seven major deficiencies. The investors argue the problems indicated the plant was not ready to be handed over.

    The December agreement itself acknowledged that repairs to the failed hot molten-salt storage tank were still needed. The tank was central to the plant's operation, storing heat from the sun so electricity could be generated even after sunset.

    CMB alleges the companies used the revised agreement to make Crescent Dunes appear ready for use and secure the Treasury grant, even though major problems remained unresolved.

    According to recent reports, electrical equipment and transmission infrastructure at the Crescent Dunes Solar Energy Project. (Michael Dorgan/Fox News Digital).

    It has been revealed that turbines used in the electricity-generation process sit atop steel infrastructure at the Crescent Dunes Solar Energy Project near Tonopah, Nevada. The plant uses heat stored in molten salt to produce steam, which drives turbines connected to generators. (Michael Dorgan/Fox News Digital).

    It has been revealed that heliostats track the Nevada sun at the Crescent Dunes Solar Energy Project near Tonopah. The mirrors concentrate sunlight onto the receiver atop the tower, visible in the distance. (Michael Dorgan/Fox News Digital).

    Records reviewed by Fox News Digital show Treasury had questioned whether Crescent Dunes was ready for use months before approving the grant payment.

    In September 2016, Treasury questioned a claim by Tonopah Solar Energy that Crescent Dunes had been ready for use since February of that year. The agency pointed to a July commissioning report suggesting the builder, Cobra Thermosolar Plants, had not yet formally handed control of the facility over to Tonopah.

    According to recent reports, in a Sept. 21 response to Treasury's questions, Tonopah Solar Energy defended its claim, arguing that the plant had passed key tests and was capable of generating electricity. It also acknowledged an earlier extended shutdown caused by problems with the plant's salt-piping system.

    The following month, the plant's hot molten-salt storage tank failed, forcing the plant offline for months.

    Despite that breakdown, Tonopah and Cobra went ahead with the revised handover agreement in December.

    On March 7, 2017, just weeks into the first Trump administration, Treasury approved a $243.7 million grant payment — even though Crescent Dunes remained shut down nearly five months after the tank failure.

    The plant would not resume generating electricity until July 2017.

    A timeline demonstrates how Crescent Dunes faced questions over its readiness for operation, suffered a major molten-salt tank failure in October 2016 and remained shut down when Treasury approved a $243.7 million grant payment in March 2017. An additional $31.9 million was approved in February 2018, bringing total grant awards to approximately $275.6 million. The approvals are central to disputed fraud allegations brought by private investors. (Fox News).

    The hot molten-salt storage tank at Crescent Dunes in Nevada. Repeated leaks involving the plant's molten-salt storage system contributed to lengthy shutdowns and financial troubles. (Michael Dorgan/Fox News Digital).

    A network of pipes and industrial equipment forms part of the Crescent Dunes Solar Energy Project near Tonopah, Nevada. The concentrated solar plant uses molten salt to capture and store heat before using it to generate steam and electricity. (Michael Dorgan/Fox News Digital).

    According to recent reports, rows of heliostats converge toward the base of the receiver tower at the Crescent Dunes Solar Energy Project near Tonopah, Nevada. More than 10,000 heliostats surround the tower across the sprawling desert facility. (Michael Dorgan/Fox News Digital).

    The receiver atop the Crescent Dunes Solar Energy Project's tower glows as thousands of computer-controlled heliostats concentrate sunlight onto it near Tonopah, Nevada. (Michael Dorgan).

    A view looking up at the receiver tower at the Crescent Dunes Solar Energy Project near Tonopah, Nevada, while the receiver is not being illuminated by concentrated sunlight. (Michael Dorgan/Fox News Digital).

    The approval letter said Treasury was still reviewing some of the project's claimed costs before deciding whether to release additional money.

    Industry observers note that in February 2018, Treasury approved an additional $31.9 million, bringing the total grant awards to approximately $275.6 million, according to newly obtained federal records. The additional payment was scheduled for disbursement within seven business days.

    But Treasury was not the only federal agency involved.

    Sources indicate that the Department of Energy, which had backed Crescent Dunes with a $737 million federal loan guarantee, also had a say in major construction decisions. DOE approved the revised December handover despite unfinished repairs. It also waived certain missed deadlines, allowing the plant to be formally recognized as operational under its loan agreement.

    That approval did not automatically qualify Crescent Dunes for the separate Treasury grant.

    A separate December 2016 financing agreement involving Tonopah Solar Energy and DOE required the Treasury grant money to go first toward repaying the project’s short-term federal borrowing, including principal and accrued interest.

    Documents obtained by Fox News Digital show that Tonopah Solar Energy made a $218.9 million payment toward a federal loan in March 2017, shortly after Treasury approved its initial grant award.

    "So in a sense, the federal government just paid themselves, right? So they're still out the money, right," Hogan told Fox News Digital.

    On April 12, 2017, while Crescent Dunes was still offline, DOE published an article celebrating the plant as a breakthrough in solar technology without mentioning that it had been shut down for months.

    What remains unclear is whether Treasury officials knew about the October breakdown, unfinished repairs and December contract changes when they authorized the initial grant payment — information that could have affected whether the plant qualified for the grant.

    Fox News Digital has asked DOE and Treasury about the grant's approval process, the plant's condition and taxpayer losses, but neither agency has provided a full accounting.

    In a statement, the Trump administration's Department of Energy criticized previous administrations' handling of the project, saying it had resolved its financial interests in Crescent Dunes in 2020.

    It has been revealed that "It is unfortunate that previous administrations irresponsibly managed taxpayer dollars in their support of the Green Newly introduced Scam," a DOE spokesperson stated. "Since 2020, DOE has had no ownership, operational, or financial interest in the Obama-era project.".

    Fox News Digital has also filed Freedom of Information Act requests seeking grant payment records, loan accounting and communications between the agencies.

    The Crescent Dunes solar plant near Tonopah, Nevada, features a central tower surrounded by more than 10,000 mirrors that direct sunlight toward a receiver to generate electricity. The Obama-era project, backed by more than $1 billion in federal support, went bankrupt twice before selling for $7 million in July 2026. (Getty Images).

    In January 2020, Hogan's investment group, CMB, which had lent $90 million to a tech giant tied to Crescent Dunes developer SolarReserve, sued Tonopah Solar Energy and companies tied to Spanish construction giant ACS, accusing them of defrauding the federal government.

    The lawsuit was filed under the False Claims Act, which allows private whistleblowers to sue on the government's behalf and receive a share of any money recovered. Known as "qui tam" cases, the lawsuits can be taken over or dismissed by the Justice Department.

    After investigating CMB's allegations for more than three years, Biden's Justice Department declined to take over the lawsuit in June 2023, leaving CMB to pursue it alone.

    According to recent reports, on Nov. 7, 2024, just two days after Trump's election victory, Biden's Justice Department moved to dismiss the lawsuit, arguing that continuing the case would burden the Treasury, Energy and Justice departments.

    CMB challenged the move, arguing that Biden's DOJ had failed to explain what had changed since it allowed the investors to proceed.

    Then, in July 2025, six months into Trump's second term, a federal judge granted DOJ's request and dismissed the lawsuit without deciding whether the fraud allegations were true.

    CMB appealed to the Ninth Circuit, where Trump's Justice Department defended the dismissal in an April 2026 court filing.

    Matt Dunn, an attorney at Covington & Burling who specializes in False Claims Act litigation, described DOJ's decision to intervene after initially allowing the case to proceed as "unusual, but not extraordinary.".

    Dunn said the government may have its own assessment of a lawsuit's potential value that differs from the whistleblower's.

    "The government might privately have a different view of the merits of the case or the potential value of the case that it doesn't necessarily share publicly," Dunn stated.

    Dunn noted the Supreme Court has given the government substantial discretion to dismiss such cases, describing the legal hurdle for whistleblowers seeking to overturn a dismissal as "an extraordinarily high bar for a relator to overcome.".

    Hogan, meanwhile, has a financial stake in the outcome. He says his investors lost the $90 million they lent to the SolarReserve-linked organization.

    If the lawsuit is revived and CMB ultimately succeeds, the government theoretically could recover up to three times its proven damages under the False Claims Act, and CMB could receive a share, potentially offsetting its investors' losses.

    "That's my job for my investors to leave no stone unturned to try to make sure that, in fact, I get their money back," Hogan noted.

    The Ninth Circuit must now decide whether the lawsuit can move forward — potentially opening the door for the government to recover hundreds of millions of dollars in disputed funds — or whether DOJ's decision to shut it down will stand.

    The Justice Department's handling of the case has also drawn scrutiny on Capitol Hill.

    Industry observers note that in February 2025, Reps. Lance Gooden, R-Texas, and Carol Miller, R-W.Va., urged Attorney General Pam Bondi to investigate why the Biden administration moved to shut down the lawsuit.

    Gooden later urged Secretary of War Pete Hegseth to consider suspending federal contracts with companies tied to Spanish construction giant ACS, whose subsidiary Cobra built the plant and held a stake in Tonopah Solar Energy. He also called for an investigation into ACS and Banco Santander's roles in the project's financing and bankruptcy amid the allegations of fraud involving federal funds.

    It has been revealed that "When taxpayers are defrauded to a scale this massive, our government has a responsibility to get the facts and hold those responsible to account," Gooden told Fox News Digital. "That is why I have asked Secretary Hegseth to pause contracts with ACS-affiliated entities until these allegations are fully reviewed and every avenue to recover taxpayer money has been pursued.".

    In February 2025, Reps. Lance Gooden, R-Texas, and Carol Miller, R-W.Va., urged Attorney General Pam Bondi to investigate why the Biden administration moved to shut down the lawsuit. (Tom Williams/CQ-Roll Call, Inc via Getty Images).

    It has been revealed that rep. Carol Miller, R-W.Va., leaves a House Republican Conference meeting in Washington, D.C., on Nov. 29, 2023. Miller has questioned the collapse of the federally backed Crescent Dunes solar plant and the potential loss of taxpayer money. (Bill Clark/CQ-Roll Call, Inc. via Getty Images).

    In a recent development, one such contract involves a $2.84 billion Navy dry dock project at Pearl Harbor awarded to a joint venture involving ACS subsidiary Dragados. The project completion date has been delayed from September 2027 to March 2029, according to the Government Accountability Office. Dragados is not accused of fraud in the Crescent Dunes lawsuit.

    Miller, meanwhile, also questioned how a project backed by nearly $1 billion in federal financing could end up selling for $7 million.

    "That's not good math," Miller told Fox News Digital. She suggested another congressional letter could be warranted, saying that "if we can recover any of that taxpayer money, that would be wonderful.".

    In April 2026, Senate Judiciary Committee Chairman Chuck Grassley, R-Iowa, a longtime defender of whistleblowers who helped strengthen the False Claims Act in 1986, demanded answers from DOJ over its handling of fraud lawsuits, particularly cases it shut down despite whistleblowers wanting to press ahead.

    In a July 10 response obtained by Fox News Digital, DOJ revealed that Crescent Dunes was one of just 12 cases in which it moved to shut down a lawsuit after initially allowing it to proceed — fewer than 0.3% of nearly 5,000 whistleblower cases received between 2020 and 2025.

    DOJ also confirmed that other federal agencies can push to have such lawsuits dismissed, including to avoid the burden of producing evidence. But it did not say whether Treasury or DOE pushed to kill the Crescent Dunes case — or what investigators found when they examined the fraud allegations.

    In April 2026, Senate Judiciary Committee Chairman Chuck Grassley, R-Iowa, a longtime defender of whistleblowers who helped strengthen the False Claims Act in 1986, demanded answers from DOJ over its handling of fraud lawsuits, particularly cases it shut down despite whistleblowers wanting to press ahead. (Tom Williams/CQ-Roll Call, Inc via Getty Images).

    The companies accused of fraud have backed DOJ's effort to dismiss the lawsuit, arguing that federal law gives the government broad authority to shut down whistleblower cases.

    Tonopah Solar Energy, which filed for bankruptcy in January 2026, has also fiercely rejected CMB's allegations, accusing the investors of pursuing a "scorched earth mission" through repeated legal challenges against the tech giant.

    "The reality is there is no merit to CMB's claims whatsoever," the company argued in an April 2026 bankruptcy filing.

    It has been revealed that tonopah Solar Energy made those arguments while winding down its affairs in bankruptcy, before selling the plant's assets in July. The upcoming owners had no involvement in the alleged 2016 fraud, and the bankruptcy sale generally shielded them from the former owner's legal liabilities.

    In a separate 2020 lawsuit, Hogan's investors sought to recover an allegedly unpaid $90 million loan, suing companies tied to Crescent Dunes after SolarReserve failed to repay much of the money. They suffered a setback in 2024 when an arbitration panel rejected five of their claims and ordered them to pay $2.44 million in legal fees and costs.

    The companies did not respond to Fox News Digital's repeated requests for comment.

    The dispute was separate from the whistleblower lawsuit alleging fraud involving the $275 million Treasury grant.

    Despite years of investigation, the Justice Department has never publicly disclosed what it uncovered.

    CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP.

    In a recent development, nearly seven years after Hogan's investors filed their lawsuit, the fraud allegations have never been tested at trial. And despite President Trump's pledge to crack down on fraud and wasteful green-energy spending, his Justice Department is still defending the Biden administration's decision to shut down the case.

    "If we're wrong, the evidence will show it," Hogan said. "But don't let a Biden-era dismissal prevent the merits from ever being heard.".

    Van Hollen: Senate rules changes a matter for caucus to decide

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Chris Van Hollen, D-Md., during a press conference on Thursday.
    • Chris Van Hollen, D-Md., endorsed a bipartisan initiative Thursday to adopt latest rules aimed at speeding up Senate procedures but stopped short of calling for abolishing the filibuster, laying down a marker on a key internal debate for Democrats as he positions himself to challenge Senate Minority Leader Charles E.
    • In a recent development, van Hollen joined Sen.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Sen. Jeff Merkley, D-Ore. looks on as Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md., during a press conference on Thursday. (Finn Gomez/Getty Images).

    Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md., endorsed a bipartisan initiative Thursday to adopt latest rules aimed at speeding up Senate procedures but stopped short of calling for abolishing the filibuster, laying down a marker on a key internal debate for Democrats as he positions himself to challenge Senate Minority Leader Charles E. Schumer, D-N.Y.

    In a recent development, van Hollen joined Sen. Jeff Merkley, D-Ore., at a press conference Thursday to express his support for a proposal from Merkley and Sen. Steve Daines, R-Mont., to, among other changes, adopt a “talking filibuster,” requiring senators to continuously hold the floor if they seek to prevent a bill or nomination from moving forward.

    Van Hollen went further to say that while his personal view is that the filibuster itself is “anti-democratic,” changes beyond what Merkley and Daines are proposing are a matter for further discussion.

    According to recent reports, “I’m in favor of filibuster reform,” Van Hollen stated. “How and when we do that is a matter for the caucus to decide.”.

    The filibuster, a Senate tactic that effectively requires a 60-vote threshold to advance most legislation, has long been the subject of calls for change or outright abolition from members of both parties.

    Other changes Merkley and Daines unveiled in October include eliminating cloture requirements for nominations and amendments, reducing post-cloture time for legislation, and introducing a new suspension process modeled after the House rules to allow bills with broad support to move swiftly.

    Merkley actually held two separate press conferences Thursday on his filibuster proposal, one with his Montana Republican co-sponsor and then later with Van Hollen, whose bid to become majority leader he has endorsed.

    At the earlier appearance, Daines said that he thought the changes, if adopted, would “truly be a cultural change for the Senate” and lead to greater bipartisanship.

    “We believe these reforms are appropriate no matter who is in the majority, no matter what the election outcomes were,” Daines said.

    Daines also reiterated his view that implementing any rules changes would require 67 votes from the full chamber.

    But Democrats have been debating whether to use their new majority in 2027 to change the rules on the first day of the session with 51 votes, or to eventually employ the so-called “nuclear option,” a series of procedural moves leading to a simple majority vote.

    It has been revealed that democrats used that tool in 2013 to lower the voting threshold for advancing some presidential nominations with a simple majority, rather than 60 votes. A Republican majority followed in 2017 by extending that change to include Supreme Court nominations, and again in 2019 to reduce the number of hours between a cloture and final confirmation vote.

    A spokesperson for Schumer declined to comment on Van Hollen’s endorsement of the Merkley-Daines plan.

    Schumer has said he remains confident in his bid to remain party leader.

    Van Hollen reiterated Thursday that his “momentum is growing,” after several senators-elect have thrown their support behind the Maryland Democrat.

    “I think people recognize that if we're going to deliver on the significant things that the American voters stood up for and voted for, you can't just go back to business as usual and status quo,” Van Hollen mentioned.

    #133940. Solar lease holdouts still see value in privately-owned residential projects

    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Solarpowerworldonline ↗ Open Full Page

    Solar lease holdouts still see value in privately-owned residential projects

    📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (978 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Solarpowerworldonline

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Industry observers note that the One Major Beautiful Bill Act drastically reduced the lifespan of federal subsidies available to certain segments of the solar market, and among the first to go was the investment tax credit for residential projects.
    • It has been revealed that A residential solar project in New York installed by Nickels Energy Solutions.
    • It has been revealed that after 2025, homeowners hoping to install solar on their house couldn’t subsidize the project’s cost with this federal subsidy if it was privately owned.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Industry observers note that the One Major Beautiful Bill Act drastically reduced the lifespan of federal subsidies available to certain segments of the solar market, and among the first to go was the investment tax credit for residential projects. The ITC is a historic renewable energy subsidy that provides a 30% tax credit against the total cost of an eligible project, and it is at the moment available to the commercial and utility-scale solar segments.

    It has been revealed that A residential solar project in New York installed by Nickels Energy Solutions. Credit: Nickels Energy Solutions.

    It has been revealed that after 2025, homeowners hoping to install solar on their house couldn’t subsidize the project’s cost with this federal subsidy if it was privately owned. However, a loophole in the tax credit language has allowed leased or “third party-owned” (TPO) solar projects to still receive the ITC (25D) on residential solar projects. In this scenario, it matters who owns the solar project, not necessarily where it’s built. The project can be subsidized because it is owned by a commercial company, and not the homeowner.

    Industry observers note that some residential solar installers are still strictly pursuing and installing privately-owned solar projects. Nickels Energy Solutions (NES), a residential solar contractor working in Central New York believes a privately-owned PV system is still the better deal for the customer.

    Sources indicate that “We don’t have the same offers as some of the bigger companies,” remarked Kevin Nickels, VP of sales with NES. “If you can offer leases, it’s like the ‘haves and have-nots.’ I don’t have that loophole or that trick up my sleeve, so it forces me to get the project sold, while I’m as sharp as I can be with margins to make it somewhat competitive.”.

    TPO solar transactions are typically arranged at a lower up-front cost than a wholly owned solar project. Lease contract lengths vary by provider, and financiers have surety in these transactions because the projects will be built with products from an approved vendor list (AVL). Products on an AVL can qualify for a domestic content subsidy, another tax credit in addition to the ITC, because they are manufactured using a certain percentage of domestic components.

    These are premium products vetted for AVLs. But it can also mean that installers are paying premium prices for components in building TPO solar projects.

    Nickels believes that, while a privately owned residential solar project will cost more at the start, the combination of expensive components and interest rates for financing over a lease term — with factors like rate increases — can cost a customer more in the long run.

    Recent findings suggest that “I don’t think all leases are bad,” he said. “I just don’t think it’s what’s best for the industry or the homeowner.”.

    Selling residential solar in 2026.

    Rudy Wright, owner of Wright-Way Solar of Tyler, Texas, has shifted the organization’s focus from building fresh projects to servicing existing systems. As the ITC exited the residential solar market, so did many of the lenders financing these projects. Without lending options, Wright-Way’s installation output has slowed down, and those clients who can afford solar are paying with cash or using a home equity loan to cover the cost.

    Despite that, Wright remarked he isn’t very interested in building leased solar projects.

    Wright-Way Solar built a solar plus storage project at a Ranch in Texas featuring arrays that are facing east, west and south. Credit: Wright-Way Solar.

    According to recent reports, “I do think it cost me some of those entry level clients, but every time I analyzed the financing end of it, I felt like I was benefitting my firm and the industry more than the customer,” Wright stated. “I haven’t seen the angle where bringing a pre-purchase agreement or bringing a lease agreement has enough ironclad return for the customer.”.

    Tyler is a unique market for solar because many of Wright-Way’s customers are trying to make their properties more resilient, and less reliant on the grid, by installing solar and storage, and not just seeking cost savings for their energy use. Wright has installed solar plus storage systems on Texan ranches at a scale close a small commercial project.

    That promise of resilience is still enough reason for some people to commission a solar project in Texas, where the state’s independent electrical grid operator has faltered and experienced dangerous outages in recent years.

    “Folks realize money in the bank doesn’t do you any good if the power goes out,” Wright said.

    NES is still building a steady pipeline of residential solar projects in New York. Nickels said that has been possible in part because many of its clients are upper-middle class; but New York also maintains an incentive program for solar projects, NY-Sun, which includes a 25% state tax credit for residential systems.

    Recent findings suggest that “The OBBBA caught a lot of states flat-footed,” Nickels mentioned. “Without federal support, it puts a lot of pressure on what the state is offering.”.

    According to recent reports, some states’ solar subsidy programs have stepped in where federal support has diminished since the OBBBA was passed. The North Carolina Clean Energy Technology Center maintains the Database of State Incentives for Renewables & Efficiency, which analyzes which states currently have policies and incentives supporting clean energy developments. Every state has policy enabling solar projects, but not necessarily cost incentives for individual projects.

    While traditional residential solar projects have lost a significant subsidy, the reality is that energy costs have risen in response to fresh grid demands from hyperscale data centers and oil scarcity from the United States’ war in Iran. Sure, a privately owned residential solar project won’t receive the ITC, but it can still stabilize energy costs without them.

    “We lost a significant incentive, but the rate increase is proportional,” Nickels stated.

    #133937. America and China Are Trying to Alter Their Economic Bargain

    📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 12m • 📚 Deep Dive (2353 w)

    America and China Are Trying to Alter Their Economic Bargain

    📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2353 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Foreignpolicy

    ⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • It has been revealed that the United States and China are locked in a derisking race.
    • Recent findings suggest that today’s derisking race signals the failure of the third attempt by the United States to build an open, fully integrated world economy.
    • Industry observers note that the United States and China are locked in a derisking race.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Get audio access with any FP subscription.

    It has been revealed that the United States and China are locked in a derisking race. After decades of actively entwining their economies, both are now trying to achieve a degree of separation between them. Neither side seeks at this point to decouple completely from its rival. Each is trying instead to alter the terms of their economic relationship, reducing their own vulnerability to leverage, coercion or attacks that could damage its long-term prosperity and security, while working to acquire advantages over its counterparty. This is a struggle for power, waged through trade, investment and technology development.

    Recent findings suggest that today’s derisking race signals the failure of the third attempt by the United States to build an open, fully integrated world economy. At the end of the Cold War, as after the two world wars, American policymakers were motivated by a mix of pragmatism and principle. They believed that there were enormous gains to be had from trade with large and potentially fast-growing markets. But they also hoped to bring to fruition the liberal dream of a ‘one-world’ global trading system in which freer flows of goods, capital and people would promote peace and freedom, as well as prosperity.

    Industry observers note that the United States and China are locked in a derisking race. After decades of actively entwining their economies, both are now trying to achieve a degree of separation between them. Neither side seeks at this point to decouple completely from its rival. Each is trying instead to alter the terms of their economic relationship, reducing their own vulnerability to leverage, coercion or attacks that could damage its long-term prosperity and security, while working to acquire advantages over its counterparty. This is a struggle for power, waged through trade, investment and technology development.

    Industry observers note that today’s derisking race signals the failure of the third attempt by the United States to build an open, fully integrated world economy. At the end of the Cold War, as after the two world wars, American policymakers were motivated by a mix of pragmatism and principle. They believed that there were enormous gains to be had from trade with large and potentially fast-growing markets. But they also hoped to bring to fruition the liberal dream of a ‘one-world’ global trading system in which freer flows of goods, capital and people would promote peace and freedom, as well as prosperity.

    Recent findings suggest that in 1919 America had the world’s biggest economy, but the international political system was still multipolar, with other great powers in both Europe and Asia. Although Woodrow Wilson tried to persuade the victors, and his own people, of the wisdom of lowering tariff barriers and creating an open global trading system, both at home and abroad he lacked the ability to compel others to accept his ideas. Once rebuffed, America drew back into isolationism and protectionism. With no nation willing and able to hold it together, in the 1930s the global economy split apart.

    Recent findings suggest that by 1945 the world had become bipolar, with the United States and the Soviet Union standing above all other nations—and America alone briefly accounting for as much as half of global GDP. American planners at first entertained hopes of reviving Wilson’s vision, but the onset of the Cold War soon forced them to abandon the idea. Instead of cooperating to create a single unified system, each superpower proceeded to build its own largely separate bloc. Organised along predominantly liberal, free-market lines, the American-led bloc was ultimately able to out-produce, out-innovate, and out-last its Communist opponent.

    It has been revealed that with the demise of its former rival, the United States finally seemed set to restructure the entire world economy into a unified trading system. America and its allies hoped in the process to encourage the domestic transformation of their former enemies, preparing them to become members in good standing of what would finally be a globe-spanning liberal order.

    Industry observers note that the main instrument of this strategy in the economic realm was the World Trade Organization, and its most crucial target was China. To gain entry to the WTO China was required to make detailed commitments that, if followed, would bring its economic policies into closer alignment with liberal principles of open markets, limited state intervention and freer trade.

    According to recent reports, political change was expected to follow close on the heels of economic liberalisation. Increased reliance on markets would lead to rising prosperity and, as had already happened in Western Europe and parts of Asia, the members of an expanding middle class would demand political rights to go with their growing economic freedoms.

    American strategists knew that drawing China more fully into an expanding world economy would enable it to accumulate power as well as wealth. But they were reassured by the conviction that prosperity would eventually bring democratisation, and by the knowledge that democracies had seldom gone to war with each other.

    In a recent development, for their part, China’s rulers saw the West’s offers of engagement as a trap designed to bring about their own demise. Instead of succumbing to the charms of liberalism, they remained firmly committed to a mercantilist-Leninist governing philosophy, in which the primary purpose of economic activity is not to enhance the welfare of the Chinese people but to bolster the power of the Party and, through it, the nation.

    Thus, even as it allowed greater play to market forces, the CCP regime took care to ensure its continued grip at home. And it approached the global economy as another domain of zero-sum struggle, one in which the aim was to strengthen China’s geopolitical position and gain advantage over its rivals.

    For a time, the nation’s leaders believed they had little choice but to accept the dangers of increasing interdependence with the West. Once having obtained membership in the WTO, however, Beijing began to take steps to reduce its vulnerability to foreign pressure.

    After the turn of the century this derisking strategy advanced along four parallel axes:.

    Recent findings suggest that to guard against the possibility of being cut off from vitally needed imports of resources and raw materials, Chinese companies were directed to buy up more overseas mines, oil wells and agricultural land and to build a vast merchant fleet and an elaborate global network of roads, railways and ports to carry their output back home. To reduce exposure to Western tariffs or trade sanctions, Beijing sought upcoming export markets in the global south. To blunt the impact of U.S. financial sanctions, it began to build alternative international payments systems. Finally, to lessen dependence on imported technology China launched a series of costly, high-profile technology development programs, began buying cutting-edge Western companies and initiated a campaign of industrial espionage of unprecedented scope and scale.

    From the end of the Cold War until the mid-2010s, Washington continued to try to ease Beijing down the path towards economic liberalisation. Together with this persistence, however, there was mounting frustration over China’s trade and industrial policies and its evident failure to live up to the commitments it had made to gain entry to the WTO. As the Chinese economy grew and its level of technological sophistication advanced, these policies appeared to threaten the future prosperity and security of the United States and other industrial democracies.

    China’s heavily subsidized exports were hollowing out portions of the American manufacturing base. Relatively easy access to Western companies and universities was helping to speed its technological advance. Its ongoing military buildup and more assertive foreign policy stance darkened perceptions of its intentions and began to make it appear less as a normal trading partner and more like a strategic rival and even a potential foe. Despite all of this, it was not until the very end of Barack Obama’s second term that China’s increasingly forceful efforts to strengthen its position finally began to provoke a meaningful response.

    Washington’s belated answer to China’s mercantilist, power-maximising economic policies signalled the start of a two-sided derisking race. The American reaction came first in the form of the experimental and at times spasmodic initiatives of the first Trump administration and then the more coherent, but also limited and cautious approaches pursued by the Biden administration.

    In a recent development, neither Trump nor Biden sought to decouple completely from China, nor did either of them formally abandon the original, ambitious goal of creating an open global economy. Nevertheless, albeit with some hesitation, at least with respect to China the United States started to move away from a predominantly liberal approach to economic relations that emphasized the virtues of openness and the prospect of mutual benefits, towards one that increasingly prioritized power and the pursuit of relative advantage.

    According to recent reports, america’s derisking campaign comprised several interrelated lines of effort. Regardless of cost, it no longer seemed prudent to depend on a potentially hostile China for minerals, drugs, metals, and chemicals that might be needed in a war or national emergency. To reduce the dangers of dependence, the United States began to use tariffs to constrict imports and subsidies to cultivate alternative sources of supply.

    Once seen as a benign byproduct of globalization, the pervasive presence of Chinese-made electronic components and hardware in America’s critical networks now appeared to pose unacceptable risks of espionage or sabotage. Dealing with the problem of penetration by removing these imported products and replacing them with reliable substitutes called for upcoming laws and regulations to guide private companies and government agencies. Finally, slowing the transfer of sensitive technologies required imposing tighter controls on exports and on investment flows both to and from China.

    Industry observers note that beijing has reacted to these developments by doubling down. Xi Jinping’s determination to stay the course is due in part to the fact that America’s tougher policies did not come as a surprise. Back in 2002, in the wake of China’s accession to the WTO and the 9/11 attacks, CCP strategists had concluded that they faced a “twenty-year period of strategic opportunity” during which they could grow strong without undue interference from Washington.

    In a recent development, eventually, however, the Americans would turn their attention back to China and, recognizing how much it had grown, they would try even harder to weaken and contain it. At that point Beijing would have no choice but to press ahead.

    In the past five years, China has done more to increase security of supplies of food and raw materials, diminish its exposure to financial sanctions, and increase the relative importance of the developing countries as markets for its exports. Together with these defensive measures Beijing has begun to take more aggressive actions. Rather than implement reforms that might have reduced exports and lessened tensions with other nations, it has moved in the opposite direction: ratcheting up subsidies, expanding manufacturing capacity, and boosting exports that threaten to destroy others’ industries and leave them even more reliant on Chinese goods. Chinese firms are also working to dominate global supply chains for critical minerals and other industrial materials. The regime has successfully used the threat of export restrictions on rare earth minerals to pressure America and its democratic partners and is actively seeking to tighten its grip on other potential “chokepoints.”.

    In a recent development, the U.S. rejoinder to this intense and purposeful campaign has been mixed and less than fully coherent. Since his return to the White House Donald Trump has expanded on some of the policies that he set in motion during his first term, but he has also taken steps that threaten to undermine their effectiveness.

    The second Trump administration has prohibited the importation of Chinese-made drones, robots, and internet routers that could be connected to U.S. telecommunications networks. But it has also ignored the law banning TikTok, a Chinese-controlled social media platform suspected of gathering sensitive information and spreading propaganda, instead negotiating a sale to one of Trump’s domestic political allies.

    Recent findings suggest that to lessen dependence on China, the administration has sought to work with other countries to develop alternative sources of critical minerals. At the same time, in hopes of reviving American industry, it has strained relations with its allies by imposing across-the-board tariffs on their exports, driving countries like Canada closer to Beijing. Finally, since returning to office, Trump has tightened certain restrictions on high tech exports to China while simultaneously loosening export controls on advanced semiconductors crucial to the development of artificial intelligence.

    China’s course in the next stage of the derisking race seems set but America’s remains uncertain. The history of the past century suggests two alternative trajectories. Having failed once again to build a fully integrated global order, the United States may choose not only to distance itself from China but to adopt a posture of omni-directional protectionism and strict “America first” industrial policy as it did after World War I. This risks leaving America isolated as its former friends band together to protect themselves from its own predatory policies as well as China’s.

    Sources indicate that the aftermath of the Second World War suggests a preferable alternative. Instead of completely abandoning liberal economic principles, Americans could decide instead to narrow the circle in which they are applied to include only those nations that genuinely share and are prepared to defend them. It is only by pooling their resources and better integrating their markets that the advanced democracies can counter a challenge of unprecedented proportions.

    Aaron L. Friedberg is a professor emeritus of politics and international affairs at Princeton University. His most recent book is The Derisking Race: China, America, and the Fragmentation of the Global Economy.

    Breaking: The U.S. Tech Outage Wave, Explained

    📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1295 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Foreignpolicy

    ⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • It has been revealed that A wave of tech outages in the U.S.
    • In a recent development, A global Microsoft outage that began last Thursday derailed a number of services that businesses, schools, and governments rely on.
    • It has been revealed that A wave of tech outages in the U.S.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Get audio access with any FP subscription.

    It has been revealed that A wave of tech outages in the U.S. federal government and private sector over the past week have made a lot of people understandably nervous. The outages affected commercial air travel, email, banking, and more—in some cases causing disruptions worldwide.

    In a recent development, A global Microsoft outage that began last Thursday derailed a number of services that businesses, schools, and governments rely on. Then the U.S. Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) issued a rare nationwide ground stop on Friday leading to widespread flight cancellations and delays. Chase Bank, Bank of America, and Apple services also faced brief disruptions in recent days. And on Tuesday, some internal systems at the U.S. National Security Agency (NSA) went down.

    It has been revealed that A wave of tech outages in the U.S. federal government and private sector over the past week have made a lot of people understandably nervous. The outages affected commercial air travel, email, banking, and more—in some cases causing disruptions worldwide.

    A global Microsoft outage that began last Thursday derailed a number of services that businesses, schools, and governments rely on. Then the U.S. Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) issued a rare nationwide ground stop on Friday leading to widespread flight cancellations and delays. Chase Bank, Bank of America, and Apple services also faced brief disruptions in recent days. And on Tuesday, some internal systems at the U.S. National Security Agency (NSA) went down.

    According to recent reports, given the outages occurred on such a massive scale and in quick succession, questions have been raised as to whether they were a result of nefarious activities. But there is currently no evidence that the recent incidents were due to cyberattacks or that they were linked.

    Recent findings suggest that the Microsoft outage was the result of a combination of factors, including a “latent bug” from July that caused servers to become “overwhelmed and unresponsive,” Charles Lamanna, Microsoft’s executive vice president of Copilot, agents, and platform, said in a post on X. Lamanna said a “surge in load” and decreased server capacity had also contributed to the outage.

    The FAA is still assessing what led to the ground stop, which lasted less than five hours, but a preliminary investigation indicated that the technical problem was caused by the installation of a router at a radio facility in Arkansas that may have flooded its communications network. A radar site in Amarillo, Texas, is also being looked at as part of the inquiry.

    The short-lived Chase Bank outage on Monday, which led to issues with processing transactions and seemingly had a ripple effect that caused problems for customers at other banks, was the result of a “software bug in on-premise hardware systems,” the bank said in a post on X, adding that “there is no evidence this is cyber-related.” Apple said the outage it experienced on Tuesday, which lasted hours and disrupted the Apple Store and other services, was the result of an “internal revision” and not due to a cyberattack.

    Industry observers note that the NSA disruption, which reportedly caused the agency’s internal communications network for highly classified information, NSANet, to go offline, had a similarly prosaic cause. “The National Security Agency experienced temporary degradation during scheduled routine maintenance,” the agency said in a statement. “While some internal systems were affected, mission-critical capabilities remain fully operational and our ability to defend national security continues. NSA’s infrastructure is designed with multiple layers of redundancy to maintain operations during planned maintenance or unexpected events.”.

    The Trump administration has acknowledged the unease the outages have caused among the public while emphasizing that there are currently no indications that any were tied to a cyberattack or coordinated by outside actors.

    Recent findings suggest that “I understand the timing of these incidents can raise questions, and it should. The American people should ask us these questions,” Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton told the House Homeland Security Committee on Wednesday. “But based on what we know today, after a great deal of digital diligence, these are separate service outages associated with maintenance and technical changes. They are not a coordinated or state-sponsored attack.”.

    Secretary of State Marco Rubio on Tuesday recognized that people are “fearful” and “uncertain,” but he was unequivocal: “We are not under systemic attack,” he said. “These events—one has nothing to do with the other. They are not interrelated.”.

    But it makes sense that people are on edge about technology and how its dominance over modern life can make societies vulnerable. All of these incidents came on the heels of a series of suspected cyberattacks on supermarket freezers in Europe that caused millions of dollars in damage. They’ve also come at a time when anxiety over the rapid development of artificial intelligence has reached a fever pitch.

    It doesn’t help that these outages hit as the increasingly symbiotic relationship between AI and the stock market was on many people’s minds amid the chaos swirling around Nvidia—following a salacious scandal that led to the resignation of the tech giant’s co-founder and CEO, Jensen Huang.

    And national security and tech experts say AI may be partly to blame for these disruptions—though not in the way you might think. AI tools are increasingly helping organizations to identify vulnerabilities in their computer systems. That’s mostly a good thing because those flaws can then be fixed before any potential bad actors can exploit them. But those fixes don’t always go smoothly.

    According to recent reports, “AI code scanning has caused a tidal wave of vulnerability discovery,” and companies and government agencies are “rushing to make updates and fix” those vulnerabilities, David Agranovich, a director for intelligence on the National Security Council during the first Trump administration, said in a post on X. “[E]specially with legacy infrastructure, it can be incredibly hard to predict all of the different dependencies that might break because of those patches. The pace of manual patching has a cost, and that cost is reliability,” Agranovich added. “The result is many cascading and disparate system outages.”.

    Industry observers note that democratic Sen. Mark Warner, the vice chairman of the Senate Intelligence Committee and a co-chair of the Senate Cybersecurity Caucus, offered a similar assessment. Warner said in a statement on Tuesday that he understood why Americans were so concerned about the widespread outages and underscored that there is “no indication that these incidents are the result of a cyberattack, foreign interference, or some coordinated effort.” But he added that what appears to be happening is a “consequence of how promptly artificial intelligence is changing the cybersecurity landscape.”.

    AI has opened the door to “identify vulnerabilities across enormous numbers of systems at unprecedented speed, creating enormous pressure on companies and government agencies to patch those vulnerabilities immediately, often all at once, putting tremendous strain on systems that weren’t built to handle that pace of change,” Warner remarked.

    The recent disruptions should serve as a “wake-up call” on the ways in which AI is “moving faster than our ability to manage its consequences,” Warner mentioned, reiterating his call for “commonsense guardrails on AI and stronger cybersecurity protections.”.

    John Haltiwanger is a staff writer at Foreign Policy. Bluesky: @jchaltiwanger.bsky.social X: @jchaltiwanger.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Sources indicate that eric Ueland, nominee to be comptroller general, sits at the witness table for his confirmation hearing with the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee on Thursday. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call).

    Eric Ueland, President Donald Trump’s pick for comptroller general, promised to be independent and impartial if confirmed, amid criticism from Democrats and outside groups, during a confirmation hearing Thursday.

    “I’m not here as a plant, a stooge, a lackey for anybody,” he told Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Chairman Rand Paul, R-Ky., after Democrats on the panel accused him of being a “rubber stamp” for the administration.

    Democrats have criticized Ueland, a longtime GOP Senate aide and administration official during both Trump terms, saying he is too politically biased to lead the nonpartisan watchdog agency which conducts investigations and audits for Congress. They also noted Republicans ignored a law that Democrats say requires the convening of a special legislative commission to make recommendations for the post.

    Recent findings suggest that ueland said if the Senate confirms him to lead the Government Accountability Office, “We can at the end of the day ... see a GAO which is more effective, which provides better information for Congress in a quicker way so Congress is able to take policy actions and drive change itself at this end of Pennsylvania Avenue.”.

    At the root of the partisan clash is a suspicion by Democrats that Trump is trying to install a puppet to lead an agency that has fought the administration repeatedly over the power of the purse and other matters.

    Democrats blasted Paul for rushing the hearing, which included a dozen other nominees for administration and judicial posts.

    Sources indicate that “It’s so apparent that this is a box-checking exercise,” said Sen. Gary Peters of Michigan, the ranking Democrat on the panel. “This committee is not doing due diligence, despite some of our members’ best efforts, because the chairman has chosen not to carry out his responsibility to provide advice and consent on nominations.”.

    Democrats noted Paul did not allow Peters to make an opening statement at the hearing and restricted the amount of time given to senators to ask questions. A GOP aide disputed this, noting that Paul did not give an opening statement himself, Peters arrived late and all senators were given five minutes to ask questions.

    In a recent development, ueland has served as deputy director for management at the Office of Management and Budget under Russ Vought, the OMB director. Trump nominated Ueland to head the GAO, a legislative branch agency, Monday.

    Democrats noted that the GAO has concluded multiple times that the administration violated the law by "impounding," or refusing to spend, appropriated funds. OMB has argued that the GAO misread the law and that it does not have any authority over the executive branch.

    Peters told Ueland that the GAO had issued 12 reports accusing the administration of violating the law, and he asked if Ueland agreed.

    Ueland did not give a direct response.

    “First, many of those items indicated by those reports, I have not participated in,” he remarked. Ueland said he had not reviewed the reports that Peters provided to him earlier, and that he would not offer an opinion on them.

    He also mentioned it was critical that he “not prejudge or come to this committee with informed conclusions about what it is that GAO has rendered as advice to Congress.” Ueland said he has a “clear commitment to follow the process.”.

    Peters remarked when Ueland appeared before the committee last year after being nominated for the OMB post, he voiced support for the presidential authority of impoundment.

    “We’re going to expect you to continue to basically ignore Congress,” Peters said. “You’re going to be a rubber stamp for the administration.”.

    “That’s not so,” Ueland replied.

    Ueland stated his experience as deputy overseeing the management side of OMB would be a “value add to GAO.” He cited his work “examining how the government actually functions, how it is organized, how it can be better optimized to deliver results.”.

    Sources indicate that sen. Bernie Moreno, R-Ohio, asked Ueland how he would grade GAO’s work to date.

    Ueland said he would give it a “medium grade over time.”.

    For example, he stated GAO has 38 government operations on a “high-risk list … some of which have been on there for 36 years.”.

    By contrast, Ueland referred to his work at OMB, where he remarked “you have seen a very swift and aggressive effort by this administration in this term to set up systems and processes to ensure that we are not sending money out the door that we shouldn’t.”.

    Paul asked Ueland what he would do if administration officials told him they did not like a GAO investigation or conclusion.

    Ueland noted he would “fully follow through on charges from Congress and in the event of obstacles figure out ways to proceed to try to elicit information.” He said when he was a young staffer in the Senate, when there were disagreements between the legislative and executive branches, GAO and the administration had conversations “to see if there were appropriate paths forward.”.

    Responding to another question from Paul as to whether he would ignore a potential request from the White House to stop an investigation, Ueland said, “To be clear, yes.”.

    Sen. James Lankford, R-Okla., who is seeking to be the ranking Republican on the committee in the next Congress, said he was satisfied that Republicans followed the letter of the law requiring a commission to make recommendations to the president for comptroller general. He added that he was not “completely sure they have followed the entire spirit of the law.”.

    In a recent development, “For me, personally, Mr. Ueland is a great candidate in this role for GAO,” Lankford stated.

    Paul sent three recommendations for comptroller general, including Ueland, to the White House last week from the six Republican members of a 10-member bipartisan, bicameral commission. But he never convened the body to seek applications from and interview candidates for the post.

    And he gave the four Democrats on the commission less than 24 hours’ notice last week to offer their recommendations. Democrats charged that Paul subverted the process, and they did not offer recommendations.

    In a separate interview Wednesday, the president of the union that represents GAO employees decried the decision not to follow the commission process that characterized past comptroller general nominations.

    “We see that bipartisan process as extremely important to preserving and keeping the trust that GAO has with the entire Congress,” noted Benjamin Emmel, president of Local 1921 of the International Federation of Professionals and Technical Engineers.

    Emmel, a senior analyst at GAO, stated by sidestepping that procedure, “there is a cloud that hangs above any nominee where one party dominates that process.”.

    He mentioned GAO’s credibility depends on members of both parties trusting that the organization is “nonpartisan, objective, independent and fair. If we lose that ability, we become less useful.”.

    In a recent development, the union is not advocating for or against Ueland or any nominee for the office. The Homeland Security panel is not expected to vote on the nominations until after Thanksgiving.
